subtopic: TORONTO-CLOSING OF DUNLOP PLANT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
TORONTO-CLOSING OF DUNLOP PLANT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 to ask for unanimous consent to present a motion.
Last Friday Dunlop of Canada announced the closing of its industrial products division in Toronto, to be phased out in a few weeks. As a result 597 Canadians, many past 40 and with long seniority, are being thrown out of work at a time of very high unemployment. The government, through two of its ministers, had been informed of the company's intention. The closing of this plant is another example of decisions by corporations without regard for the effect on the lives of Canadians and
on the community and without adequate notice to the employees concerned. It is urgent that the facts of this case and the entire problem be studied in depth by a committee.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin):
That the closing of the Toronto industrial products plant of Dunlop Canada Limited be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Forest (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):

speechtext:
I am informed by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and the Department of National Defence as follows: 1. Yes, the Education Division, the Judicial Division and the Census Division of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics collect some information on reading deficiencies and illiteracy among Canadians.
2.	As of January 1966, 12,108 children were being provided special remedial reading programmes in special education facilities, including both those operated by school boards and those run by other organizations, in which specially-trained teachers were employed. This is not to be taken as an indication of the percentage of children who can be classified as retarded readers1. A common finding of researchers is that 3.4 per cent of the population can be classified as retarded.
3.	In Canada's adult population (20 years and over), according to the 1961 Census, there were 169,904 illiterates with no schooling (1.63 per cent of the population), and 828,597 who were functionally illiterate, with one to four years of schooling (7.93 per cent of the population).
4.	According to the 1961 Census 13.4 per cent of the unemployed, aged 15 to 19, and 10.4 per cent of those aged 20 to 24, were functionally illiterate, with less than five years of elementary education.

5.	In 1967, 8.32 per cent of juvenile offenders were functionally illiterate (1,499 of 18,000 juvenile delinquents who had been to court). Of those who entered Training Schools in 1967, 12.83 per cent were functionally illiterate (312 of 2,431). These are not necessarily the same people who appeared in court.
6.	The minimum acceptable education standards for a male applicant for enrolment in the Canadian Forces is Ontario Grade 8 or equivalent, and for a woman Ontario Grade 10 or equivalent. He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-190 has been placed before the House to enable a number of necessary and desirable amendments to be made to the National Energy Board Act. The Act was first passed in 1959 and has not been amended since 1963 except for matters which were consequential to the passage of other legislation by Parliament. For instance, the passage of the Statutory Salaries Revision Act in 1967 included such an amendment to the National Energy Board Act.
The amendments now proposed in Bill C-190 are a reflection of changing circumstances and the experience of the board in discharging its important responsibilities since the last amendments in 1963. I hope it will be helpful to hon. members if I take just a few minutes to outline some of the more important changes proposed.
Before I do so, perhaps I should remind hon. members of what the board does. It is responsible for adjudicating upon applications for licences to export and to import natural gas, applications to construct and operate inter-provincial and international pipelines for the transportation of petroleum and its products and of natural gas, and applications for licences to export electrical power and energy and to construct and operate international power lines for the transmission of such power. It is responsible for regulating the rates, tolls and tariffs of pipelines under its jurisdiction, a field into which it is just now entering and which will require a great deal of careful attention in coming years.
It recommended to the government of the day what became the national oil policy, established in 1961, and the board has administered that policy since its inception. It has advised successive governments on a wide range of matters having to do with energy, and has assembled a small but highly competent staff expert in the disciplines of engineering, finance and accounting, and operations research as they apply to oil, gas, pieplines and electrical power.
The Board and its staff have earned and have the confidence of the government, and I believe that of businessmen and members of the general public in Canada who have come into contact with their work. In my present responsibilities, I have come to have a high regard for the capacity and judgment of the board, and to rely upon it as a principal source of advice in the many matters relating to energy which require the attention of government. We are at the moment in the midst
March 9. 1970

National Energy Board Act of particularly complex considerations about oil, but I do not foresee a time when the judicious resolution of difficult questions relating to energy will not be an important concern for any government of Canada. For such resolution, I believe the National Energy Board to be necessary and effective.
I turn now to the substantive amendments incorporated, along with many minor or relatively incidental changes, in the bill now before you. First, let me explain the proposed amendment in respect of international power lines.
Both Canadian and United States power utilities are now placing increasing reliance upon transmission connections with other utilities to achieve additional security of supply, economy of operation and earnings from surplus energy. In an increasing number of cases, such interconnection arrangements are becoming advantageous and desirable as between utilities in Canada and utilities in the United States.
The high voltage interconnection between power systems, one on either side of the international boundary, is normally used for the importation of power for one interval of time, followed by the exportation of power for the next interval. In other words, it is seldom used only for a one way flow of power, whether import or export, but rather it is used for both, as the occasion warrants.
The increasing exchange between the two countries is borne out by the trade records. In 1960, Canada exported some 5.5 billion kilowatt hours, and imported some 0.4 billion, for a net export of 5.1 billion. In 1969 the preliminary figures are that Canada exported about 4.7 billion kilowatt hours but imported 3.3 billion, for a net export of only 1.4 billion kilowatt hours. To put this in perspective, the total supply of kilowatt hours in Canada in 1969 was 194 billion.
As the Act now stands, if a Canadian utility proposes to construct an international power line for the purpose of exporting power, it must obtain a certificate of public convenience and necessity before constructing and operating the line. On the other hand, no present provisions of the Act prevents that utility from constructing a major transmission interconnection if the initial intention is to import power. The line having been constructed, when the time comes for it to be used for the export of power, the board is faced with an ex post facto application which leaves it with no opportunity to deny the certificate and little power to include condi-

tions respecting the route or the adequacy of the specifications for its construction, having regard, say, to the public safety.
The government believes it would be in the public interest that the board be given jurisdiction over international power lines constructed and operated for the purpose of importing power on the basis comparable to the jurisdiction which it now exercises over export power lines. It proposes, therefore, that the Act be amended to require that lines to be used for importing power, as well as those to be used for exporting power, may be constructed and operated only pursuant to a certificate of public convenience and necessity issued by the board. There is no intrusion Whatsoever over the existing line of demarcation between the jurisdiction of the provinces over the electrical utilities within their boundaries, and the jurisdiction of the government of Canada over international connections established by such utilities.
At the present time, the importation into Canada of liquified natural gas by any means other than through a pipeline does not require a National Energy Board licence. In 1959 trade in liquified natural gas was not significant, but there have been rapid technological advances. Plans for the importation of liquified natural gas into eastern Canada by tanker or other non-pipeline methods are being developed and, since it appears that the scheme of the Act is to make subject to licencing restrictions any import or export of natural gas which may affect the public interest, the government considers that it would be appropriate that importation of liquified natural gas should be subject to licencing control.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
To put it another way, it would be as imprudent to allow an area or community to become dependent upon tanker-borne liquefied natural gas as it would be to allow the same community to become dependent upon natural gas moved internationally or inter-provincially by pipeline, unless it had been demonstrated that the service was reliable, economic, and otherwise consistent with the public interest. There are, in addition, considerations as to safety in the handling of liquefied natural gas which would be more readily safeguarded if its importation were subject to licence. It is proposed, therefore, that the existing authority of the National Energy Board to licence the import of gas be extended to include liquefied natural gas by amend-
March 9, 1970
ing the definition of "import" to include importation by railway tank car, tank truck or by tanker as well as by pipeline.
The Act now empowers the National Energy Board, when issuing a certificate in respect of the construction of a pipeline, to prescribe such terms and conditions as are considered necessary or desirable in order to give effect to the purposes and provisions of the Act. It is proposed to make manifest the Board's power to impose requirements respecting preservation and restoration of land through which a pipeline may be constructed by amending section 46 of the Act as proposed in Bill C-190.
It has been brought to the attention of the Board in public hearings, and through representations made in the House and to ministers of the Crown, that dissatisfaction has existed among farmers with the interference with and the impairment of both municipal and private farm drainage systems which may be created by the construction of pipelines. This is particularly so in those areas where the installation of tile and other types of drainage is necessary to carry on efficient agricultural operations. Through the Board's hearing and decisions, and through consultation with various agricultural associations and with pipeline companies and the pipeline division of the Canadian Petroleum Association, greatly improved practices by the pipeline companies have been established. As a result, I believe relations between the agricultural community and the pipeline companies are now much better than at some times in the past.
With respect to new pipeline construction, the Board has applied the concept that gravity land drainage systems should take precedence over pressure pipelines. To ensure that the same concept may be applied to existing pipelines, it is proposed that where the Board finds that such pipelines interfere with or otherwise impair the proper operation of public or private drainage systems, either existing or proposed, it be empowered to direct a pipeline company, upon such terms and conditions as the Board considers proper, including the specific power to direct by whom the cost should be paid, to divert, relocate or otherwise reconstruct the appropriate portions of its pipeline so as to remove the existing interference or impairment or to otherwise facilitate reconstruction or relocation of drainage systems. I should add that a number of pipeline companies have already 21774-10
National Energy Board Act voluntarily undertaken remedial action of this sort where it appeared desirable.
Since November, the Board has been involved in the most lengthy and arduous hearing since its establishment. This hearing arises from applications by five applicants for certificates of public convenience and necessity and licenses for the exportation and some incidental importation of gas. The decisions on these applications will be highly important to the development of the Canadian natural gas industry for some years to come. At the same time that this major gas hearing has been before the Board, it has also been considering ten other applications for certificates respecting the construction of pipelines and international power lines or for licences for the export or import of propane or for the export of power. The Board has held five public hearings with respect to certain of those applications. Others are still to be set down for hearing when the applicants have satisfied the Board that the data in support of their applications is complete and the application is ready to be heard.
In October 1969, the Board found it advisable and in the public interest to bring into effect, as provided for in section 97 of the Act, its authority over the regulation of rates, tolls and tariffs of certain oil and gas pipeline companies which were not previously subject to the Board's jurisdiction in this regard. A major application by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited respecting rates has already been filed with the Board, and increased activity in this area of responsibility is to be expected.
Because of the increase in the Board's workload arising out of its regulatory function in respect of certification of pipelines and international power lines, its licensing functions in respect of the export of gas and power and import of gas; the impending activity in regulation of rates, tolls and tariffs of oil and gas pipelines; additional responsibilities arising out of its advisory functions, and in keeping close surveillance over new developments in the energy field; and in recognition of the additional responsibilities proposed to be placed upon the Board by the amendments to the Act set forth in Bill C-190, the government is of the opinion that the membership of the National Energy Board should be increased from five to seven, with provision for the appointment of an Associate Vice-Chairman from among the Board members.
This increase in membership would enable the Board to conduct two public hearings

March 9, 1970

National Energy Board Act upon applications at once, and to reach decisions upon applications in shorter time than has been possible under existing circumstances. Three members constitute a panel for the public hearing of most applications. I say "most" because there is provision under section 14 of the Act for one member of the Board to be authorized to hear and report to the Board upon a matter. It has, however, been found in practice to be desirable to limit the use of this power to relatively simple issues; in most certificate, licence and rate matters the issues are complex and important enough to require the hearing and analysis of the evidence by three independent minds. With five members it is impossible to have two concurrent hearings, and with the present and foreseeable hearing load it is becoming increasingly difficult to hear and decide with reasonable dispatch all applications coming before the Board. If only for the sake of maintaining reasonable expedition in deciding applications to the Board-and of course each of these applications represents a matter which is urgent and important to the many people affected by it-it is therefore desirable that the number of Board members be sufficient that two panels can operate at any one time.
Thus far, on this matter of the number of members, I have been addressing myself only to the regulatory work of the Board. As I indicated early in my remarks, we also call upon the Board for advice on many matters. Board personnel have carried a very heavy responsibility in the preparations for and the conduct of the discussions which for many months have been taking place between officials of the United States and Canadian governments. There is no indication that the need for such discussions will diminish. Often these matters have to be dealt with urgently, and it is not easy for the Board or for me to deal with them promptly if the Board members whose advice I want are tied up in a formal hearing. I, therefore, look to the increase in Board membership to provide more flexibility in the time of the members.
Similarly, it seems to me important that we increase the membership of the Board to enable it to give more attention to the long range implications constantly arising for future Canadian energy policy and problems. Here, the obvious example is the new developments in the North. Hon. members may recall that the chairman of the Board is a member of the task force on northern oil, which we set up after the Prudhoe Bay discoveries but before the discovery of oil in the


Mackenzie Delta and of gas in the Arctic islands. The development of these northern discoveries, and the related transportation and marketing problems, are matters that require sound and prompt advice to government. One means to obtain such advice, I submit, is to have available two more men with the capacity, objectivity and dedication which are expected of members of the National Energy Board.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In the bill now before you there are a number of other amendments. I would not describe any of them as unimportant, for the need for them has emerged in the light of experience, and in many cases after intensive discussion with knowledgeable people such as the members of the legislation committee of the Canadian Petroleum Association and executives of the Canadian and Ontario Federations of Agriculture. However, the remaining amendments are of a kind which, with deference, I would suggest could more appropriately be explained and discussed in committee where I and representatives of the board will be pleased to answer questions and explain whatever may need explaining.

Obviously this has not been the minister's day in the House. I confess that I believe he would have liked to have answered the questions I put to him on the previous bill, but somehow or other the information was not there or else it was better to obscure the true purpose of that bill.
In dealing with this bill, let me say first of all that I am conscious of the fact that the National Energy Board has been in existence now for about eight or nine years. It was as a result of the Borden Commission report that the board came into existence. The government took the advice of the Borden Commis-
March 9, 1970

sion and set up the National Energy Board. Those of us who were in the House at that time will recall that the creation of this board was breaking entirely new ground and, as a matter of fact, did not meet with universal acclaim. There was some concern in the various parts of the country, depending upon the form of energy that was prevailing or predominant therein, that certain types of people would tend to dominate the board and that primarily electric power utility experts would be dealing with gas and oil.
At that time, the chief problem facing the government of Canada was the question of the export of natural gas, and great pressure was being exerted. We were indeed fortunate in obtaining the services of Mr. Ian McKinnon, who was chairman of the Alberta Oil and Gas Conservation Board, and who came to the public service of Canada first of all on loan and then permanently, to establish the board and to lay down the general lines of conduct. He was fully experienced as the chairman of a form of utility commission, and I think that Canada gained a great deal by this appointment. Now that Mr. McKinnon has retired, I am sure that all of us expect to see the same high standards of performance by the National Energy Board that it has maintained in the past. When called upon to explain matters to members of Parliament, particularly those who form part of the delegation of the Canadian American inter parliamentary group, the Board has filled them in on the situation, and have done so also in the delicate situation concerning oil and gas between Canada and the United States.
There are other problems of course which we cannot neglect, such as the question of water power and the export of electricity and other forms of energy. There is the very difficult situation with regard to uranium and its processing and export for power and energy purposes.
The minister made some very brief comments regarding the performance of the board and its ultimate purposes. I would have liked to have heard him say a good deal more about the national oil policy. I know that there are some problems at present regarding what the decision of the United States may be concerning the level of Canadian imports. Of course this decision will determine the nature of the national oil policy.
There is one thing that I do want to point out, since I come from an area that is more than vitally interested in the marketing of Canada's oil production. Within our own 21774-10i
National Energy Board Act domestic market there are recurring rumours, and reports which go even beyond rumours, that the national oil policy boundary with respect to the marketing of Canadian products along the line of the Ottawa River is being breached by refined products coming from refineries in the Montreal region and in other parts of the country. In addition, with the establishment of the refinery at Port Hawkesbury and the proposed refinery near Quebec city, as well as the proposed refinery in Newfoundland, there will be an ever increasing pressure on the marketing of Canadian oil products by products having their source in off-shore crude. This is bound to happen.
It is not that western products that are already in those markets will be replaced. It is not that the refined products themselves from, say, the refinery that is to come into existence at some time-and this may be a long way off, but there are progress reports which may be mere flack reports for the purpose of keeping up a pretence-will replace western production, but in any event there is no doubt that they will displace other petroleum products within the Canadian structure and gradually there will be a push westward. Naturally, the barrier which will be established by the national oil policy will come under the greatest and strongest pressure. Unless the market west of Ottawa increases substantially to absorb the natural increase in the western production, we will either have to maintain a rigid policy-and I do not know how the board may police this- or ancillary action may have to be taken by the government to police this so-called boundary line and the actions by the oil refineries or the petroleum distributors so that the Canadian production will not suffer unduly.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It is not only the producers of the crude and the refiners who are adversely affected by the diminution in the marketing of Canadian petroleum products, but at least three provincial governments have a great stake in the revenues derived from the royalties and other dispositions of oil and gas rights. There is, of course, the other point about the United States and Canada's rather delicate position at the present time. I don't want to say too much about the negotiations. Certainly, I would not want to say anything that might be prejudicial in arriving at a possible solution for Canadian producers. But it seems to me that with the requirements of
4536	COMMONS
National Energy Board Act the United States for gas, and there is a vast increase in them,-the minister spoke about the increase in applications before the National Energy Board for the export of natural gas-that it would only take a limited amount of enlightened self-interest to see that the marketing of both gas and oil are inextricably linked. There is no question, Mr. Speaker, that most of the natural gas in the past has been found as a result of exploration for oil. If there is going to be a ready market for the gas reserves there is no question one can view with equanimity the rapid accumulation of unproductive oil reserves, or drilling operations that result in a successful well which is merely capped because there is no market for the oil.
There are many operations in western Canada at the present time that are marginal or less than marginal, and unless there is a very strict quota system with respect to operations, many operations will be definitely shut down. True enough, there are many others now who are going out for the exploration of and have found natural gas, and that is their prime purpose. I think we may see a pattern of change in the exploration.
These are problems of very great significance in the field of energy, and yet we see an indication in the white paper on taxation of the government moving in like a bull in a china shop with the taxation of the operators in that field of resource development, without seemingly taking in what they are doing with regard to the ultimate disposition of the end product. It seems to me that when you look at the two points of view they are in distinct-at least in the goverment's eyes-separate chambers having no relationship whatever.
I can readily understand that in the minds of a number of people who have never seen an oil well, all you have to do is open up a drilling company or get out on some exploration program, sink a bit in the ground and, just like Little Jack Horner with that plum pie, by merely sinking a thumb in, out will gush all that is good. It is only an absolutely naive myopia that prevents individuals from understanding the problems of the oil and gas industry and understanding that all is not rosy. True enough, the people in the area certainly may work and get good wages and salaries, but so far as the profits are concerned, in many instances, they are merely sunk with the shareholders' money in holes in the ground. I think I will leave that particular point.
However, we are at the present time, Mr. Speaker, moving into some areas of pressure.

DEBATES	March 9, 1970
I asked some questions this afternoon with regard to the fact there seems to be a movement towards the development of a continental energy policy. I don't think anybody is yet in a position to fully realize the implications of a continental energy policy which would involve water, and when one considers it strictly from certain points of view it makes complete sense. On the other hand, I can readily understand there can be arguments completely on the other side with regard to a continental energy policy, and I am sure we will have to give this matter very, very grave and serious study.
Just as an indication, I recall a few years ago when the first export of natural gas took place from Alberta to a copper refinery in Montana. It was felt that this had to be on a fixed period because there was a great deal of money being invested by Anaconda, and they had to be given the opportunity of paying off the capital cost of the installation. But strangely enough, it is much like a small boy who has been given a good treat. As soon as that period was finished or that the flow was appreciated, back they came and said, "More". We have seen a continuing appetite for gas through this particular connection. The same may be said now of the existing pipelines, oil lines and gas lines to the Pacific coast. In addition we see, of course, the extensive requests for natural gas to be piped into the central and east central United States.
There are no two ways about it. This is not an interruptable service. We must clearly understand that the greatest possible persuasion, and not only persuasion but force, would be applied to Canada if for some reason or other in the national interest it came to the point of turning off that gas unless of course appropriate stipulations are made beforehand and are clearly understood. After all, we know what kind of pressures can be brought to bear. At the time the Canadianization of Time magazine was taking place the American government clearly pointed out to the Canadian government that negotiations for oil market quotas in the United States would be completely broken off if Canada did not place Time magazine and Reader's Digest in the most favourable position they are in today.
This is a question of relationships between neighbours, I will agree, but while I come from Alberta and am fully cognizant of the economic worth of these disposals of oil and gas to the United States to that province and to Canada's position in international trade- there are so many advantages-on the other hand I am also wondering, and I put this up
March 9, 1970	COMMONS
as a signpost to observe and to examine, about the danger of getting locked into a situation where there would be no getting out even though in 20 years, the situation may have changed so much that Canada would be at a considerable disadvantage.
And so I conclude with those few remarks with regard to the question of present negotiations, the present situation and the difficulty but necessity of establishing a national oil policy. I must confess that the past few years have not been the most exemplary with regard to a national oil policy. I have always been very critical of the reason for all of this secrecy about the so-called secret accord of 1967. The present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has never been fully able to explain it. He has tried to dissimulate any criticism but frankly he has failed in that regard.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
With regard to the present bill there is a great deal of tidying up of definitions to be done. All I can say to that is that it is lawyer's load and of course, this can be readily understood. Over the past ten years of experience with the board, I am sure the committee has come up against certain definitions which were not as flexible as they wanted, nor as accommodating. In any event, I do not think there is much to be said about the definitions part of the bill.
As to the composition of the board, I am glad the minister went into detail and I think the change is quite understandable. If there had been, concurrent with the recent series of hearings with regard to the gas export applications, other types of hearings with regard to the export of electrical energy or the question of uranium, or if there had been problems with regard to the export of water power. I do not know what would have happened. Somebody would have had to queue up because the board was not in a position to deal with that situation. I think the move to get seven members, to have two panels, is a move in the right direction. It is only natural to expect that this board, since Canada is developing more and more of its energy resources, would have more to do. This board, from being a fledgling in matters of this nature, will now assume a much more important role.
Earlier this day we had a bill which set aside the Dominion Coal Board, writing its obituary if I may say so. Although many years ago the Dominion Coal Board was a very important body, with the passage of
DEBATES	4537
National Energy Board Act time and the evolution of technology it was no longer necessary to maintain it. I think in many ways it has been replaced by the National Energy Board since we have now moved to other forms of energy.
Of course, the success of this expansion of the board will depend upon where the emphasis will lie with regard to the skills of the two additional members. I would have liked to have heard from the minister, if he would listen on this particular point, where the emphasis will lie with regard to the expansion of the board. Are these people to be oil and gas specialists or utility men or what is going to be their particular specialty? I have nothing much to say about having an associate vice-chairman. Because of the mechanics of the expansion, it is understandable that there should be one.
There is one rather ironic thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the minimum salary scale for members of the board, whose skills are matched by a great many members of this House, is more than double the salary scale for members of this House.

I think as far as getting qualified personnel for the board is concerned, the minister is quite right. I am glad to see that he set minimum salaries for the positions. I think in order to get appropriate men one has to be in a position to deal with a competitive industry. This is not a case of picking up engineers or specialists coming out of university but of getting men who have established themselves, have made a reputation and have the capabilities and qualities required on such a board. The salaries should be high enough. I think they should range in the level of the Exchequer Court and the Supreme Court of Canada. Having said that, I am sure there are men in this House who have just as much capability and who work just as hard and contribute just as much to this country, yet their salaries are in a somewhat different range.
There are two or three points I should like to make, Mr. Speaker. In clauses 7, 12(3) and 28(3), the board is not allowed to hold public hearings or may not hold public hearings, as the case may be. In clause 7, it is clear by the language in the section that the Board is not to hold public hearings. That may be very well but I will say this: There is no reason why the findings of the board or the decision of the board with the reasons therefor, should
March 9. 1970

National Energy Board Act not be made public. If the minister will take particular note of this point, it is in the case where either the holder of a certificate consents to it or where the pipeline or international power line to which the licence relates, has not been brought into operation under that certificate or licence.
Notwithstanding the fact that you certainly cannot have private hearings, I do not see the value of any necessity for public hearings. Surely, the respect for this board, as the respect for any other board, lies in the openness of its decisions. It seems to me that notwithstanding the fact there shall have been a private hearing, there is nothing that commends itself with regard to not publishing the decision. Therefore, I would hope the minister would see fit to authorize the board to publish its decisions and any reasons therefor.
Clause 9, and this was a point on which the minister spent some time, refers to the diversion of a pipeline so that it will not damage a farm drainage or a water drainage system. I would say that, in addition to the fact that the board can direct by whom and to whom the cost of diversion or relocation should be paid, there should be specific provision that under no circumstances should it be the farmer or the owner of the drainage system who shall pay any costs.
The last question I want to raise, Mr. Speaker, is with respect to the purpose of clause 19, that is, permitting any pipeline company, in the acquisition of land, to acquire the minerals thereunder. If you will recall, under the original act, mines and minerals were exempted from any acquisition of land. I think it would be instructive to read section 69 as it is now:
A company is not entitled to mines, ores, metals, coal, slate, oil, gas or other minerals in or under lands purchased by it, or taken by it under compulsory powers given to it by this act, except only the parts thereof that are necessary to be dug, carried away or used in the construction of the works, and except as provided in this section, all such mines and minerals shall he deemed to be excepted from the conveyance of such lands.
At times I have thought that provision constituted some little intrusion into the field of property and civil rights, particularly in those areas which use the Torrens system, as in Alberta, where the question of the rights arising under the conveyance are specifically covered by the Land Titles Act of the province of Alberta. Notwithstanding everything that has been said on the subject, I do not see how amended section 69 could in any way abro-


gate any rights of acquisition under a conveyance properly drawn up, executed and registered under the Land Titles Act of the province of Alberta or the equivalent act of Saskatchewan or Manitoba. The amendments, as proposed, are permissive. I can see why, if under an order of the National Energy Board a right of way was granted on the surface of land for the construction of a pipeline, it was intended that that in no way was to be deemed as conveying to the company any interest to mines or minerals, with the exception perhaps of subsurface gravel which would be used in the construction of the pipeline. I can see that a pipeline company could specifically negotiate for, and indicate in the terms of its contract, that it is acquiring the right to mines and minerals. This amendment now empowers the company to acquire them, and I can see where this may happen.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I can that at its tank farm, and we have many in Edmonton, a pipeline company with facilities which occupy a fairly vast area would not want an outsider coming in and drilling for oil or gas on its site. Yet, this is actually what could happen. I say that because if the act previously prevented the pipeline company acquiring the rights to mines and minerals and these rights were in the hands of a third party, the third party could negotiate with another exploration or oil development company and an application would be made to the Alberta Right of Entry Board to go in on the land. True enough, it might be at a pretty high cost. I still feel that, unquestionably, a government body or other body should grant right of entry for the purpose of drilling for oil, gas or even sulphur on the land the pipeline company has acquired for major installation purposes. I do not know whether there is anything to be gained by acquiring the rights to minerals underneath the right of way of the pipeline system.
I agree with the minister that there are many technical explanations that can be given in committee. I hope when we see this bill again for third reading, after it has been before the committee, that there will be more clarity with regard to the future of the national oil policy and with regard to our position vis-a-vis the United States. This has become very worrisome and could have grave consequences in Canada on our balance of payments, the level of employment and the revenue of both federal and provincial governments, especially if there were a major cut

back in our oil marketings in the United States. We know this is an election year and that there are all sorts of difficulties down there in this regard. I think it our government negotiators, and particularly those representatives who are going to Washington tomorrow take a tolerably firm stand, and all the interests in this regard do not lie on the one side, I am sure our United States counterparts will be made to see that the world does not revolve round their domestic orbit at all times. We hold many cards and intend to develop our oil, gas and energy resources for Canada's interests first. Then we will, I think, be quite prepared to consider the requirements of our neighbours.

I should also point out that some of our provincial premiers have been responsible for our failure to develop a national policy in this field. All too often they have been anxious to lay their hands on a fast buck, especially just before an election, and have neglected the long run interests of the nation. In some parts of Canada the premiers seem to wear blinders and do not see the long run interests of the nation. An example is to be found in British Columbia. We know what happened with regard to the Columbia River Treaty. Another example is to be seen in the fact that we have allowed the Japanese to come in and develop a resource without paying any regard to the future of the province concerned.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It may look great in the lifetime of Premier Bennett, but the question we have to ask is: what price will have to be paid by those who will come after us? It seems to me the federal government has not been forceful enough in expressing its opinion and standing up to some of the provincial premiers. We see this situation in a province such as Alberta, where everyone's thinking seems to be dominated by oil. One would think nothing else existed in this country except oil. The more oil they can sell, the better it is; they do not care about the conditions. Just sell oil; nothing else really matters. Manitoba is the only province which has shown any sense, any willingness to work in the national interest. I think other provinces would do very well to seek to emulate the statesmanlike stance of the premier of Manitoba.
In Alberta, we find a government which prides itself on the fact that it does not need to impose a sales tax. It points to the other provinces and says: They all have sales taxes, but look, we don't. What the people there fail to see is that because of the national oil policy, because of the myopic-minded way in which we approach the selling of our oil,
4540	COMMONS
National Energy Board. Act every Canadian pays tribute to Alberta, and this is why the province is not obliged to impose a sales tax. There can be no doubt that the national oil policy has resulted in the higher cost of gasoline throughout the country. It has been estimated that it costs 5 cents more for every gallon we buy as a result of this national oil policy which keeps one province happy.
Then, there is the foolish policy under which one province is pitted against another in connection with resource development. An industry goes to a province and says: Either you give us the advantage of special concessions or we will locate elsewhere. Provinces fight each other over the right to have their riches despoiled. How long will this sort of thing continue? I know it can be said that a good deal of the fault rests with the provinces themselves, but in my opinion the main fault lies with a federal government which has never asserted itself, which has allowed the matter to drift because it had no policy.
In this country we are always being told how intransigent is the Province of Quebec, how difficult it is to get along with Quebec, how Quebec is threatening confederation. I would suggest with respect that other provinces have been as guilty, if not more guilty, of contributing to the strains within confederation. The federal government has permitted this to go on by failing to take a stand. Sooner or later we must face up to some of these provincial gauleiters. The country does not belong to them, nor do the provinces belong to them. In any confrontation, particularly in English speaking povinces, between the federal government and the provincial governments, I think the people of Canada would opt for the federal government, would opt for nationhood in preference to narrow partisanship in one particular part of the country.
The federal government has failed to produce a policy concerning foreign ownership. The consequence is that a branch plant economy is doing virtually what it pleases in Canada. Operations of companies here have been integrated with those of parent corporations in the United States and in other parts of the world. This may make sense for the companies concerned but it does not make sense for Canada. For Canada, it has meant loss of control.
It is a temptation to view every situation as a crisis and to see every piece of legislation as a watershed. But the forthcoming negotiations on a continental energy policy do, indeed,

DEBATES	March 9, 1970
represent a watershed. We can no longer delay the development of an overall policy regarding the use of Canadian resources. It has been said by people who work in the communications field that we have perhaps ten years in which to solve our problems or else go under as a nation. We could go under even faster by following a resource policy which takes no account of the long range national future.
The minister is sitting very quietly in his place today, although usually he is much given to making outrageous accusations against anyone who does not recognize his omnipotent wisdom, or anyone who dares suggest there might be other ways of doing things.

speechtext:
One thing to which our party takes objection is any policy which would make it impossible for Canadians to create their own kind of society-any kind of continentalism which would tie us in so tightly with the United States as to make it virtually impossible for us to develop anything unique or desirable on our part.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who comes from an oil province and who has a great deal of interest in seeing exports of oil increase, express the fear of a Canadian nationalist that we have not always bargained strongly enough and that there are conditions under which we should not succumb to pressure. He cited the example of Time and Reader's Digest in the case of which one slight threat that oil imports would be cut off was sufficient to legitimize two magazines and frustrate attempts to develop a Canadian literature and a Canadian journalism.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We in this party have been too long concerned over human welfare, and over the future of this country, to want to see that aborted by a continental energy policy that would make any kind of freedom to live our own lives impossible. We will object to placing our affairs in the hands of business corporations, whether they be American or Canadian, that really do not care about the society in which we reside so long as they can make a dollar. It is not only international American corporations of which I speak; some Canadian corporations are equally guilty. The unfortunate fact is that the Canadian government

National Energy Board Act has let them do as they pleased, and this cannot go on. It is one thing to have a continental energy policy that ensures that corporations have some concern for the future of this country. It is another thing to have a continental energy policy that permits corporations to go across the border and act without giving any thought to the future of this country, being interested only in their own balance sheet.
It may be that, if a continental energy policy is to work, we will have to set up marketing boards through which to sell our energy-our oil, our gas, and perhaps our electricity. It may also be that in order to make this policy work and to ensure that Canada receives the maximum benefits from such an arrangement we will have to take the oil industry under public ownership as the only way to ensure efficiency, to ensure that that industry will operate in the national interest. The minister may respond by saying "Socialism!" It may be that the only way to survive as a nation is to bring in national policies, whether they are socialist or otherwise.
The argument about socialism stifling free enterprise does not cut much ice any more with people who are interested in this country. They are asking which way they can best survive, which way they can best serve the interests of Canada. If we cannot meet these objectives-and I do not think we can-by allowing international oil companies to take over our industry, then it may be necessary to bring the oil industry under public ownership; and if this appears to be the course we should adopt, we should not hesitate to do so.

speechtext:
Our party will object to a policy that permits people who use our energy resources to pollute and despoil our environment, to dehumanize society, and then to walk away and leave the government to pick up the pieces. This is what they call efficiency. They think this is a good way to run an industry, and that governments are always wrong. Governments do spent far too much money, and one of the reasons is that they have to pick up the pieces after other people have made the profits. This sort of thing cannot be allowed to continue.
In any energy policy there will have to be a very clear understanding that these most important conditions to which I have referred will have to be met. Certainly, I for one am
March 9, 1970

National Energy Board Act not prepared to see the people of a nation that has ruined its own resources, polluted its air and befouled its rivers, move into Canada and do the same thing with our resources. It is true that we have pollution problems too, but we are going to solve those problems. As I say, I am not prepared to see other people who have flung their own resources away in the interest of a materialistic society, and without caring a damn for the future, given a licence to do the same thing in this country.
We object to bailing out another society that is in serious trouble because it has not exercised wisdom in the use of its resources. As long as 10 or 15 years ago a report was issued in the United States indicating a serious shortage of resources was developing in that country. There was another story in this morning's Globe and Mail confirming how serious is the shortage of resources and energy in the United States.
Again, I want to make it very clear to the minister and to those in his party that we cannot stand by and say to one nation whose resources are being depleted, even though it has been foolish in the use of its resources, "Ah, you have acted badly; don't come crying to us". They are still neighbours of ours, and I think we will have to sell some of our resources to the United States. I think arrangements will have to be made to transfer energy to the United States.
Having said that, my concern is that we transfer these resources on our terms. I am not suggesting we should put the United States up against the wall and tell them we will get the last ounce from them; that is not what I mean. But there does have to be a very clear understanding that resources in the world are scarce and that they cannot simply be flung around. If the United States does have access to our energy, then they will have to adopt policies that are somewhat more reassuring than their present ones.
We also think there has been a lack of balance and emphasis in regard to development of secondary manufacturing in this country. In the long run, it is not good enough simply to continue to plunder resources, because resources become depleted. Since the United States has developed into a manufacturing nation, that country would be in great difficulty if it had to depend merely upon its natural resources.
We have to get rid of a tax system that gives bonuses to the mining and oil industries which should not be given. If we are going to sell our resources, particularly when they are 
in tremendous demand, then we should at least get some value from them. When a tax system makes special concessions to resource industries, if those resources are sold then some of the benefit that might accrue to Canada will be lost. For that reason, we should make certain that there is no bonusing of the mining and oil industries. Even though the white paper does suggest some changes for these industries, very substantial handouts to the natural resource industries still remain.
So that the minister clearly understands our policy and does not go around spouting a lot of stuff that does not make any sense, I should like to express our position as it is found in these four major points.
First of all, before any continental energy policy is concluded, the minister must ensure that the use to be made of Canadian resources will be made a matter of public policy; that the decision will be made by the government of Canada acting on behalf of the people of the country, instead of the decision being made by the large corporations of the world.
Second, that there will be a real benefit to Canada from such an energy policy, a benefit that is long term, not a short term, quick meal of pottage.
Third, in any energy policy negotiations all matters affecting trade will be discussed, not merely energy. Energy cannot be discussed out of context with other areas of trade in this country. It is true that the United States wants to discuss energy alone, but we should be prepared to insist upon discussing all matters affecting trade at this time. If we bargain away our energy resources, we may never have another chance to discuss those other areas of trade that are so vital to the nation.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
One of those matters that has to be discussed is the access of Canadian manufacturers to the United States. The United States has a great deal going for it in Canada. This is a beautiful set-up for them. There are no tariffs against raw materials because the United States desperately needs raw materials. They take all we can give them, but try to sell them some manufactured goods except those in respect of the Canada-U.S. auto trade pact. Perhaps there are some, but they are relatively few. These companies have then-branch plants over here which are not permitted to export back to the United States. Let us develop agreements with the United States, because Canadian companies, by
March 9, 1970

agreement, are restricted to the Canadian market. Let us have access to the greater United States market.
One of the problems facing Canadian secondary manufacturing industry, and this is a problem which perhaps would not have faced it if the United States had not come in and virtually destroyed our economy with their branch plants, is the fact that they are blocked from the United States market. Now that they have wrecked our economy with their branch plants and destroyed our efficiency by blocking our manufacturers out of United States markets, at least in respect of most manufactured goods, they have made it virtually impossible for us to develop secondary industry. There should be no export-let me not say "no". I am not prepared to see an enlargement of our energy exports to the United States unless there is some substantial give on their part in the matter of access to their markets for our manufactured goods.
Another matter that needs to be discussed with the United States is the question of then-wheat policy. While we are going around being nice boys and signing wheat agreements, the United States is cutting our throats on price. This has got to stop. If you are going to be neighbours you are going to be neighbours. This is one of the problems that must be discussed with the United States before any agreement can be concluded on an energy policy.
Fourth, and most important, there must be a clear commitment from the United States that their laws will not apply to Canada. We are tired of the intrusion of the United States law into Canada causing infringements of our sovereignty. I have in mind their trading with the enemy laws. If their companies are Canadian they are going to have to obey Canadian laws. That must be clearly understood. There must be an end to extra-ter-ritorialism on the part of the United States. Surely, no nation that calls itself free, and that looks to have a future, can tolerate the kind of intrusion that has taken place in Canada by the United States government.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is most important as we head into negotiations on a continental energy policy that we be very clear about our objectives and very determined to see that irreparable damage is not done in the course of these negotiations or the agreements that might arise from them. I believe it is possible to have an integrated policy on energy with the United States, but only if the
National Energy Board Act needs and interests of Canada are met in a fair way.

I suggest right from the start that it will be very difficult to get the large international oil companies to consider the best interests of Canadians unless we enter these discussions and considerations with a very fair attitude ourselves. We certainly cannot expect a one way deal. We must look at the tremendous resources of energy, whatever they may be, natural gas, petroleum products, electric power, or some of the new, sophisticated sources of power which we anticipate in the next 25 to 50 years. These will include atomic reaction and other forms of nuclear power, including solar energy, which are only now coming to the fore.
The whole subject is complicated because there is a time element involved. We need, as anybody who has studied the white paper will be well aware of, large sums of money for the development of our own country. The government of the day is looking desperately for these forms of revenue. We are discussing the necessity of taxing profits no matter where they are and quite rightly, particularly excess profits or profits not in the best interests of the people of Canada. Certainly, through the white paper, all branches of governments as well as industry itself should take a look at this.
In order to sell any forward looking policy we have to be good salesmen, and a good salesman has to know the people to whom he is selling his ideas. I do not think the kind of speech we have just heard represents a good start if we expect the United States to come to us, particularly in view of the fact it has most of the bargaining on the short term policy in its hands. As far as we are concerned, the United States controls the large international oil companies. It is principally these United States companies which at the present time

would just like to make a comment or two on the speech of the member preceding me before I start on my remarks. When he referred to a continental oil policy and to U.S. ownership, I had the feeling that perhaps I should touch my forelock in the approved method of a peasant saluting the owner of the land. I think that we in this party do not criticize the Americans for making a good business deal in investing in Canadian oil. We realize they have good business heads. This is my attitude in reference to the remarks just made.
We favour the improved regulations envisaged in the bill. I suggest that before we go overboard in selling such things as power abroad we take an adequate inventory of the resources we have. This is particularly true of natural gas. We should check what we have in the way of power resources against Canada's possible future needs and make sure that our future requirements are adequately protected. I can well see us selling bottled natural gas from some of our oil wells in the Arctic at the same time as the oil. If we must export power in any form I favour its export in the form of electricity rather than as oil, natural gas or uranium because this means that some jobs will be given to Canadians in constructing an utility.


Hopefully, we will get a return in investment, and I am assuming that any sale of electricity will pay us dividends or will be to our advantage. Surely, this would be the case because if not, what would be the point of selling our power to anyone? The only market abroad for Canadian electricity at the moment is the United States. We have heard repeatedly that they have an increasingly greater need for electricity. If we can sell power to our advantage, it might be better to do this than to sell it in the form of natural gas.
I should like to deal specifically with the sale of uranium of which Canada has plenty. If we could sell atomic energy plants abroad, hopefully sales of uranium or enriched uranium, plutonium or thorium might follow. In effect, we might be making a better business deal than by selling a raw, natural resource power which someone else converts in their factories. What I am saying to the minister is that perhaps we should look for a better business deal than we have in the past. I have a great deal of respect for the business ability of the Americans. They have not achieved what they have without having a fair knowledge of business and displaying a good deal of business ingenuity. When you are dealing with a horse trader of this kind you should use some caution.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO ALLOW EMPLOYEES DEDUCTIONS FOR LIVING EXPENSES WHILE ABSENT FROM PLACE OF RESIDENCE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act, section 11, subsection (9a) by deleting after the word "where" the words "the employer's establishment to which he ordinarily reported for work was located" and substituting the words "he maintained a self-contained domestic establishment in which he resided and actually supported a spouse or a person dependent upon him for support and connected with him by blood relationship, marriage or adoption.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will not repeat the private members' notice ol motion No. 12 standing in my name in today's Order Paper. The motion to amend section 11 (9a) of the Income Tax Act, which I have the honour to present to the House this afternoon, is based on a brief to the Royal Commission on Taxation submitted by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees' Association on behalf of the employees of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool engaged in construction and repair of country grain elevators, annexes and cottages, and made with the full knowledge and support of the employer, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the original submission dealing with this problem was made directly to the Hon. E. J. Benson, Minister of Finance, on August 25, 1969, in a letter by Mr. G. A. Mills, Secretary-Manager of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees' Association.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The purpose of the motion I am presenting today is to allow employees incurring a necessary and legitimate expense for meals in the carrying out of the requirements of their employment to deduct these expenses from their taxable income. At present expenses incurred for board, or received by them for board, are included in computing their taxable income.
The situation I am concerned about is that of the employees engaged in the construction and repair of country grain elevators. After submission of a brief to the Royal Commission on Taxation, some relief was obtained by a ruling of a chief assessor to the effect that those construction employees engaged in
Income Tax Act
"new" construction could come under exemption by reference to section 5(2)(a) of the Income Tax Act. Although welcome, this ruling created an even more obvious discrimination in that workers employed by the same company, often engaged in work of a similar nature at the same site, are in some cases allowed to deduct the value of their expense allowance from their taxable income and others are not.
For example, and as related to the employees of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Association, there is the situation at Gainsborough where repairs to the pool elevator were carried out in November and December of 1968. The work performed included installing electric motors in crib annex, east frame annex, and on head. A complete new boot was installed and metal liners were put in auger box. This is but part of the work that was done there, but as this work was not classed as new construction these men were not allowed to deduct their living expenses while at Gainsborough from their taxable income. Had they built a new elevator at the station, their expenses would have been deductible.
The motion I propose would provide an equitable solution to this problem. It is only since 1961 that these workers have not been allowed to claim expenditures for meals as an expense deductible from income. From 1951 to 1961 these employees were allowed to claim as a deduction from income the amount expended for meals during the period they were required to move to different places in the course of their employment
The 1961 ruling not to allow deduction of meal expenditure was made by the Department of National Revenue Taxation Division. This ruling is based upon section 11 (9a) of the taxation act, holding that the work site at which employees are engaged is the establishment where they report for work and therefore they would not be away from the employer's establishment to which they ordinarily report for work.
I do not dispute the legality of the interpretation placed on section 11 (9a) of the act by the legal authorities. They have, no doubt, given the wording very close and careful scrutiny and consideration. However, the refusal to consider claims for meal expenses is based entirely upon the words "where the employer's establishment to which he ordinarily reports for work was located." The fact is that the elevator construction and repair workers may work one day at Buffalo

March 9, 1970
Income Tax Act
Gap, the next day at Big Beaver, and the next tour days at Yellow Grass, the next two weeks at Estevan and the next two weeks at Spring Valley. In fact, having completed one day's work at Big Beaver they may not return to that place in the next two or three years. Nevertheless, the department maintains that Big Beaver is the establishment to which these workers report for work "usually" or "generally" or "as a rule." This is a situation which must be corrected.
The department has also ruled that the non-allowance regarding claim for meals that applies to the construction and repair workers does not apply to their foremen. This creates a rather peculiar situation. A foreman, and one of his workers living next door, may be sent by the company to repair an elevator 100 miles away. While on this assignment the foreman's expenditures for meals are deductible from his taxable income while his helper, working under the same circumstances but for a lower income, has no such privilege.
It is no doubt such unjustifiable and plainly evident discrimination and inequity, that prompted the Carter Commission to make this observation, and I quote:
The self-assessment system of taxation is only a viable system if taxpayers believe that everyone is bearing his fair share of the tax burden.
The motion before you is aimed at just that. I express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will see fit to adopt this motion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO ALLOW EMPLOYEES DEDUCTIONS FOR LIVING EXPENSES WHILE ABSENT FROM PLACE OF RESIDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in the debate. But first of all, we must admit that the point raised by the hon. member has not much significance. There is a point of law I wish to discuss, but I must say that the hon. member is talking about an exception to an exception, because subsection (9a) of section 11 refers to an exception to subsection (9) which in turn refers to an exception to section 5 of the Income Tax Act.
One can see that the Income Tax Act deals differently with the income of a wage-earner and that of a tradesman or someone who is self-employed.
Indeed, a self-employed taxpayer may deduct most of his expenses. If he has to go to another city for something related to his business, he may deduct the cost of his meals. If he takes to lunch someone who will help him in his business, he is entitled to a deduction. All he has to do is establish that such expenses are related to his work in a sense
[Mr. Southam.'l
acceptable under ordinary accounting principles.
On the other hand, in the case of a worker who earns a salary, he must find in the Income Tax Act-and this may take much time and effort-a section which spells out the deduction which he is entitled to.
For instance, section 5 stipulates as follows, and I quote from the English version:

Income for a taxation year from an office or employment is the salary, wages and other remuneration, including gratuities, received by the taxpayer in the year plus

A list follows detailing what must be added. As for what may be deducted, instead of having a general accounting formula, there is a very specific list of what can be deducted.
Speaking of the case mentioned by the hon. member, I say it is a striking example of how specific the law is about allowable deductions. The basic rule is that the salaried employee is not allowed any deductions. Then, there is a list of the specific items that may be deducted.
Subsection (9) reads as follows:
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

(9) Where an officer or employee, in a taxation year,
(a)	was ordinarily required to carry on the duties of his employment away from his employer's place of business or in different places,
(b)	under the contract of employment was required to pay the travelling expenses incurred by him in the performance of the duties of his office or employment, and
(c)	was not in receipt of an allowance for travelling expenses that was, by virtue of subparagraph (v), (vi) or (vii) of paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 5, not included in computing his income and did not claim any deduction for the year under subsection (5), (6) or (7).

This is the case of one of those employees referred to by the hon. member.

there may be deducted, in computing his income from the office or employment for the year, notwithstanding paragraphs (a) and (h) of subsection (1) of section 12, amounts expended by him in the year for travelling in the course of his employment.

I shall deal now with what can be deducted. Subsection (9) does not deal with the cost of meals. However subsection (9a) says the following:
March 9. 1970

Income Tax Act

(9a) An amount expended in respect of a meal consumed by an officer or employee shall not be included in computing the amount of a deduction under subsection (6) or (9) unless the meal was consumed during a period while he was required by his duties to be away for a period of not less than 12 hours, from the municipality where the employer's establishment to which he ordinarily reported for work was located and away from the metropolitan area, if there is one, where it is located.

Let us suppose for instance that a construction worker is employed by a company whose head office is in Big Beaver and that he has to work 100 miles from Big Beaver and stay there less than 12 hours, and that his employer does not pay him any travelling expenses. I must tell you incidently that if the employer pays him travelling expenses, section 5 (2a) applies then but it is a different case.
If the employer provides no allocation and the employee has to pay his own expenses, the latter is entitled to the deduction. Under the change proposed by the hon. member, in order to be entitled to the deduction it is sufficient for the worker to earn his living alone. If he works, not only at a great distance from his boss's office, but far from his usual residence, he is entitled to the deduction.
Under such circumstances, a general deduction may be justified if expenses are incurred by the worker in the process of earning his living. But the proposed amendment generates another type of injustice because, as I have told the member, it is only necessary to work in a location away from home. So, if a man lives 100 miles from Toronto but works in the latter city, he will be entitled to a deduction under the terms of the amendment moved by the hon. member. It may be argued that he is entitled to a deduction under these circumstances, but is it not a fact that the man who lives in Toronto and performs the same work should be allowed the same deduction?
There is something else to be considered in the latter's case. We come to the abnormal conclusion that the unmarried worker with no dependent is not entitled to the deduction. In fact, the amendment merely states that the worker must live far from a town where, and I quote in English:

-he maintained a self-contained domestic establishment ... in which he resided and actually supported a spouse or a person dependent upon him for support and connected with him by blood relationship, marriage or adoption-

Only those in the circumstances described will be entitled to the deduction. Where, indeed, one must ask, is the justice of this? Clearly, a man's living expenses are the same whether he has a family, lives far from his place of work or is single.

The government proposes to make more provision in the law for the expenses legitimately incurred in earning wages or salaries. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was suggesting that when a commodity, in this case energy, is in demand in the United States or in some other area, we try to obtain a better deal than we have been getting. For example, we might tie gas sales in with oil sales; we might make one sale conditional upon the other. Gas is in demand and is in relatively shorter supply than oil. If we are to export gas to the United States, we might try to make oil sales part of the deal. I think this would be good business. Our neighbours to the south, the Yankee traders, are pretty shrewd businessmen and would probably do something of a similar nature if the situation were reversed.
I should like briefly to discuss another idea. Rather than move our energy such as water, gas, oil and power to the big cities or other places for manufacturing purposes, sometimes it might be more sensible to move industry and people to the sources of energy. It would seem to me to be only reasonable that on occasion we consider this approach.
Cities are becoming congested; traffic is a continual problem. We have built up urban ghettos where there are crime waves and a network of social problems which the smaller centres do not have. Recently I read that
March 9, 1970

National Energy Board Act industry in Great Britain has been encouraged to move out into the country or to more rural areas. It seems to me this would be a sensible approach to take in this country, at least in part. We might on occasion move the people and industry to the power, rather than moving the power to people and industry in the cities.
The United States is proposing a continental energy policy. If the United States really believes in this policy on a reciprocal basis, I think it would behoove that country to encourage some industry to move to our sources of energy rather than expect our water, power, gas, and so on to move to centres of United States industry. If the United States really believes in a continental policy, and if Canada has an advantage because of our raw materials, we might conceivably use this as an approach in solving the over-all problem of industry in North America. I strongly suggest that we use our abundance of energy resources as a lever in order to make a better deal in respect of any future agreements with the United States.
If private business will not develop industry in Canada, where there is a great amount of natural and relatively cheap power, I suggest we look carefully into having the Canada Development Corporation build industry in these resource areas. We could tie our industrial growth in with private industry in this connection. As an example, when the CCF government was in power in Saskatchewan it underwrote the bonds in order to finance the building of the pipe plant in the city of Regina. This was a private enterprise backed by provincial government funds. That plant is a particularly productive and going concern. In fact, at the present time in Saskatchewan, where much of the industry is stagnant, this particular industry has expanded.
Just a few days ago an oil man suggested to me that if a decision were made to build a pipeline from the Mackenzie basin to Chicago, they did not know where they would obtain the pipe with which to build the several thousand miles of pipeline required. In the development of industry in Canada I think there is room for more and continued use of our own energy resources. Instead of importing many of the required items, I think we should take advantage of the opportunity to produce more of them ourselves. In this regard I believe that in co-operation with business we might be able to create the industries to produce some of these items. However, if private enterprise is not interested, I would sug-

gest that in a federal company sense we might ourselves build some of these plants.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
We should seriously consider this approach rather than just making a deal whereby we give away our raw energy resources to the United States and do not receive an equivalent long-lasting benefit in return. In effect, we will be hewers of wood and drawers of water forever, in the economic sense, if we do not adopt such a policy. If we want to convert Canada into a modern, industrial state we will have to look seriously at some of these aspects in regard to power in our own country.
