maintopic: OIL AND GAS PRODUCTION AND CONSERVATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, APPLICATION, OIL AND GAS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is very important because of its principle and substance as shown in clauses 3 and 6. Clause 3 makes it clear that the principle of Bill S-5 applies "in respect of oil and gas in any of the following areas", and then it states that these include the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. The clause then provides:
-or if the administration of the oil and gas resources in the area has been transferred by law to, any of the ten provinces of Canada.
From that clause we clearly understand the intent of the government to apply the principles of this bill to practically all the areas of Canada included in the provinces and the territories. Clause 6 covers a vast field
March 9, 1970

because it authorizes the minister or such other person as the Governor in Council deems suitable to exercise such powers and perform such duties as may be necessary for the removal of oil or gas from any area that is outlined in clause 3.
As I said, it is not only an important bill because of its provisions under which a great deal of authority can, will and undoubtedly must be exercised, but it is one in which I find myself keenly interested from an historical point of view because in discussing clauses 3 and 6 we are dealing not only with matters of drilling and pollution but also those of jurisdiction and sovereignty.
In making my own small, personal contribution to the debate I should like to touch on all these factors. As I said, I am keenly interested in this matter because, if my memory serves me correctly, some 25 years ago I moved a motion in the British Columbia legislature foreseeing the problems that have developed in the past quarter of a century and asking that the province of B.C. and the federal government get together to discuss the question of jurisdiction and sovereignty. My motion asked that they go into all the details of the issuance of licences, fees for drilling and the question of royalties; and if they could not get together or reach a satisfactory conclusion, that the matter be referred to the Supreme Court, and pending a decision of the Supreme Court that the government, temporarily at least, exercise jurisdiction but put the money into escrow until such time as the Supreme Court reached a decision.
I mentioned that matter to show that my interest is not new in this most important phase of our economy, and is not just a first interest in the act, the principles of which are espoused throughout the length and breadth of this country. Other speakers have mentioned time after time the dangers of oil pollution and the requirement for the powers which are outlined in this bill. I believe it is not possible to overemphasize the seriousness of oil pollution. It was only recently that the Society for Pollution and Environmental Control put out a most interesting and factual document. Mention has been made of then-report by other speakers, but I feel that as a certain amount of detail was not given I should take the opportunity at this time to mention it.
As I say, a study was made and a report was published. I hope it was sent to all mem-21774- 11
Oil and Gas Act
bers of this House, because in the analysis of the problems and dangers of oil pollution to Canada they pointed out a significant, but I think not too well known fact, that in the three years preceding the wreck of the Torrey Canyon 91 tankers were stranded in various parts of the world and 238 tankers were involved in collisions. If we make a breakdown of the record of this society, we find that in the world at large tankers have been involved in potentially serious accidents on an average of twice a week. According to the available information, during the past 10 years 488 tankers of 30,000 tons dead weight or more that are registered with the American Bureau of Shipping were involved in 573 collisions, an average of one a week, and in 43 of these accidents oil pollution was a possibility.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I think that in order to understand the importance of this bill and the principles contained therein we should note the facts which are available to us, especially the knowledge that the largest number of accidents of tankers carrying oil-83 per cent of them in the last ten years-occurred either close to shore or in ports, areas of the greatest economic, aesthetic and nutritional importance to mankind. We also have to keep in mind that the size of tankers is ever on the increase. Unfortunately, as we have learned to our bitter regret from the experience of recent days and weeks, there is a lack of technology on how to handle oil spillage and oil pollution. But particularly is there a lack of knowledge and technology in handling oil spillage or pollution, tanker collisions or collisions with icebergs in cold weather and Arctic waters. I was most interested recently to read in more than one scientific magazine that scientists state that the potential biological and environmental damage which could result from oil spillage would be most serious in Canada's Arctic. The scientists maintain that the climate will prolong the existence of spilled oil and oxidation and dispersion, which may take several months in temperate climates, will take years in the Arctic.
These reports have been the reason for some of the knowledge I have acquired in recent months. Because of the statements being made by our own scientists and others, because of the future development which we can foresee in the Arctic, particularly with the new field opening up with the second voyage of the Manhattan, I am glad that at

Although many months and indeed years have passed, there is no indication of an intensification in recognizing the necessity of working out the most minute detail of the differences between the provinces and the federal government, of working out a method of administration and management. I sincerely hope that as a result of the introduction of this bill-I am certain of its acceptance in principle-we will see as a necessary step, a corollary to this bill and the application of its principles, the working out of the problems which still exist. Of course, that is just a problem of jurisdiction within the boundaries of our country. We have also heard a great deal, and will in the future, about the question of sovereignty over the Arctic waters.
I am glad that there seems to be a growing tendency on the part of the government to make clear to all countries what it maintains is Canada's sovereignty and that it intends to enforce Canadian laws and regulations-there will be many new ones under Bill S-5-relating to the maintenance of water quality and pollution prevention and control. I maintain that we require even more action than we have seen in recent weeks in order to make our sovereignty known in unmistakable terms to all countries of the world.
We know, or should know, that the continental shelf doctrine states that the resources of the sea bed and subsoil belong to the nation. That principle was incorporated in the United Nations Geneva Conference on the Law of the Sea in 1958. Although it is a little more debatable, I think we have an additional argument on sovereignty where this bill will have a great impact, and additional strength in that the World Court in 1951 held that the base lines system was permissible and legal and that a country was justified in using it even though the waters which were formerly part of the high seas became subject to domestic ownership. This also became part of the Law of the Sea by the 1958 Conference of the United Nations at Geneva.
If this bill is to mean anything, if its objectives are to be accomplished, I hope we will immediately work out our problems regarding jurisdictional administration, division of royalties and other questions of financial return.
I hope we will more emphatically make clear the sovereignty of our waters; that we will keep in mind the absolute importance for the future of our country and of mankind to enforce laws regarding the dangers of pollution, and to acquire the technology necessary to control it when it occurs.
21774-Hi
Oil and Gas Act
Mr. Speaker, as I draw to a conclusion I should like to emphasize, not in my own words because I have read words that explain it much better than I can, this fact. I remember, as I think the majority of us do, the adventure of the sea lion which a few years ago escaped into Lake Ontario from a zoo at a Canadian summer resort. I remember reading a comment on that misadventure which said that the sea lion lived for several months in Lake Ontario and died shortly after it was recaptured. The reason for death was malnutrition. There was general public sympathy for the sea lion, but I believe there should have been more concern over the condition of our lake in which the sea lion starved to death. I cannot think of a better commentary on why we in this House of Commons, with our responsibilities, should not be paying the deepest attention to these matters and to a bill with implications and principles such as we see in Bill S-5.
So this evening, Mr. Speaker, when man boasts of reaching the moon, let us hope he does not forget the oceans and rivers and streams that flow by our door. It is indeed a strange fact, that while we are probing outer space for other forms of life, we are neglecting one of the foundations of our own existence. I say it is time we smartened up, and I think this bill is a step in the right direction.

maintopic: OIL AND GAS PRODUCTION AND CONSERVATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, APPLICATION, OIL AND GAS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my voice to those of the many members who have spoken in this debate on the dangers of pollution in Arctic waters. It is a very serious problem and one which this country must meet very quickly.
This bill is pertinent in two ways. It would be pertinent to the possibility of oil pollution in connection with drilling on the sea floor, and it would be pertinent in relation to the pipelining of cured oils from island to island, to the mainland or to seaports in Baffin Bay. If the Panarctic consortium should strike a large deposit of oil at Banks, Melville, Ellesmere. Axel Heiberg or one of the other islands of the high Arctic, we would face the problem of pipelining it out on the sea floor, if that should prove possible, or of finding some other means of transportation.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
However, Mr. Speaker, that which has most interested Canadians recently, the voyage of the Manhattan, is not affected by this bill. It is to this aspect that I wish to address these

March 9, 1970
Oil and Gas Act
few remarks. I am a little disturbed by the course the debate has taken. As I said earlier, I share completely the feelings of many hon. members who have spoken and who are afraid of the havoc which could be wrought in the north by oil pollution. Unfortunately, instead of leading the House into a discussion of this bill which is designed to give Canada control of operations on the sea bed, several hon. members have turned this debate into one on our sovereignty over the Arctic waters. I see no connection between these two subjects.
I shall refer briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) who moved the amendment to hoist this bill for six months, and the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) which followed. On February 13, as reported at page 3590 of Hansard, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said:
I think there are two matters that have to be considered seriously, not as to the detail or content of the bill itself, but as to its general effect. The first is what I consider a derogation of the sovereignty of Canada in our northern waters by virtue of a definition in this bill.
On the same day, as reported at page 3595 of Hansard, the hon. member for Peace River, in referring to the bill said:
In my opinion it could have a serious affect on the Northwest Territories. Both by expression and implication it amounts to a serious diminution of Canadian sovereignty over the waters of the Arctic.
Other than being concerned with operations on the sea bed such as drilling, which may pollute those waters, I contend this bill has little to do with the waters of the Arctic. It does not affirm our sovereignty over the Arctic waters between our islands either negatively or positively. That is an entirely different issue. I do not want to belabour the point but, briefly, there are three areas of concern touching our sovereignty in the north.
One area concerns our sovereignty over the land, and there I think our concern ought to be practically zero because we are not chal-legend at the moment, and provided we are not so foolish as to lose interest in our northern islands and give them to other people our sovereignty there is assured. The second area of concern has to do with the waters between the islands. I have spoken at length in this House on the matter because I am very concerned about it. I feel that by way of a declaration that they are internal waters or territorial waters, the government ought to exert control over the Northwest Passage.

We must be in a position to inspect oil tankers or submarine tankers which may go through in the foreseeable future. This country, and this country only, is in a position to exert that sovereignty. However, this is not what Bill S-5 is concerned about. It relates to the continental land mass of the Yukon and Northwest Territories as well as the Arctic archipelago which lies above it. Originally, the bill said nothing more. When it returned to this House, subclause (b) had been added to clause 3. It reads:
-those submarine areas adjacent to the coast of Canada to a water depth of two hundred meters or beyond that limit to where the depth of the superjacent waters admits of the exploitation of the natural resources of the sea bed and subsoil thereof-
That is nothing more than the commonly accepted definition of continental shelf formulated at the 1958 Geneva Conference. It relates, and I cannot stress this too strongly, solely to the sea bed and minerals which may be found on or beneath it. As a matter of fact, an interesting example has been put forward by international legal experts and it is based on this definition of the Geneva Conference. The example has to do with a continental shelf and its resources. The question that was asked was: Do those rights which extend to the subsoil and soil of the continental shelf extend to the marine life which may be on the shelf?
There was a dispute as to whether one's rights extended to a lobster. Some said that a lobster may not be part of the shelf's resources but a crab is, the argument being that the crab continues living on the sea bed while the lobster flits free, so to speak, of the sea bed and therefore is not necessarily part of the resources of the sea bed.
Hon. members may think I am raising a trivial example. Perhaps it is trivial, but it is very pertinent to the point that the sea bed convention concerned itself with waters lying above the sea bed. The rights alluded to relate purely to mineral exploration and development and, to a very minor extent-so minor that I imagine it is of little concern in the Arctic-to any life which may be permanently on the sea bed itself.
I therefore feel that the submissions of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and the hon. member for Peace River may mislead those Canadians who are concerned about our having sovereign control over the Northwest Passage and who think we ought to decide regulations governing the safety of any ships which might pass through it.
March 9, 1970

My closing remarks will touch on the subject of pollution. In previous remarks I alluded to the passage of the Manhattan and other supertankers through the Northwest Passage, and to the possibility that drilling for oil on the continental shelf may expose us to the hazards of oil pollution. The Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development recommended very strongly that there be immediate research in Arctic waters to determine what the effect of hydrocarbon pollutants will be in those waters, because we do not know. As a matter of fact, the world is grossly uneducated as to the effect of hydrocarbon pollutants in any waters.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Even more so, we lack knowledge of the way in which these oils, particularly crudes, will behave in waters whose temperature ranges from 29 to 31 degrees Fahrenheit over most of the year. How long will they persist? What will be their action in the waters of the eastern Arctic, for example, in Lancaster Sound which is open for a few months of the year and lightly covered by winter ice for much of the year? It is only about this time of the year that the ice freezes to a depth of 12 feet.
What would be the effect further over in the M'Clure Strait which the Manhattan failed to negotiate, where the polar pack comes in with a depth of 20 feet, extremely hard ice built up in many layers? Perhaps while we are discussing this bill I should not mention shipping, since nothing is said in it about the passage of ships. But supposing there should be a spill from a pipeline into these waters: for how long would the oil be trapped beneath the ice? If it moved, where would it move?
I questioned the minister one day as to the committee's report. I must say his answer was of less than statuesque simplicity. He said many departments were involved and he hoped all would be well. I questioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) another day, and he suggested that in connection with the research now being carried out in Cheda-bucto Bay where the Arrow ran aground, Dr. Ian McTaggart Cowan might be able to extend his investigations north into the Arctic- perhaps! If that was not the meaning, it was the intent of his statement.
I was not satisfied with the answer given by either minister. I think it is pertinent to our discussion of this bill to strongly urge that the minister should prevail upon his col-
Oil and Gas Act
leagues, whether upon all five of them or upon whichever combination might be necessary, that they should quickly institute these studies. Knowledge is power. We need power to control pollution in the Arctic. Let us begin by seeking knowledge quickly-this year, this summer. Surely, studies can begin this summer on a subject which is not only of benefit to this country but is of potential benefit to the warm water countries of the world as well as to those nations which have polar seas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken before on the National Energy Board Act amendment. I find myself drawn into debate on the bill before us now because it is closely related, as to jurisdiction, with the National Energy Board measure. I am not saying that the National Energy Board has the jurisdiction which might be given to some body, for example a conservation committee, under this legislation. There is some question, of course, as to the exercise of control over pipelines. If a pipeline were to cross an interprovincial or interterritorial boundary, it would come under the jurisdiction of the Energy Board. I find myself wondering how the two bodies would resolve a conflict of jurisdiction or opinion with regard to a pipeline matter.
I was further drawn into the argument by the speech of the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) who has just completed his remarks. He has in my opinion totally misread the import of the remarks of my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and my hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). The act does make its own the wording of the Geneva Convention regarding the continental shelf. We must clearly understand the purpose of the act passed last year. It was an act defined as being for the protection and conservation of oil and gas as applied to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Now someone has said: We must tack on provision for the continental shelf wherever it may exist.
I do not think there was any doubt in anyone's mind as to the purpose of the act passed last year. Now it no longer applies. The whole northern purpose of the act is out. Not only is the title changed, but the emphasis has been broadened. Not only is it to control the production of oil and gas on land and on shore, particularly in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, but now we have added the continental shelf.

March 9, 1970
Oil and Gas Act
It is at this point that my hon. friends, both sound lawyers, if I may respectfully say so, say there has been introduced into the definition of this act an element of doubt. The Parliamentary Secretary, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange), and my hon. friends have all made reference to this question. Let us see just what the wording is.
(b) those submarine areas adjacent to the coast of Canada to a water depth of 200 metres or beyond that limit to where the depth of the superjacent waters admits of the exploitation of the natural resources of the seabed and the subsoil thereof.
This takes one out beyond what might normally be the surface territorial limits. It also introduces the possibility that there might be areas in the north where waters are deeper than 200 metres and where the superjacent waters would not admit of the exploitation of the natural resources of the sea bed and subsoil. This is the point. When the entire area under examination has not been explored and the precise depths have not been established, it becomes very dangerous to introduce definitions of this type into the act.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
If the definition had had two parts, firstly, the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and secondly, those coastal waters outside or not contained within that sector, you would then have two areas that were clearly mutually exclusive. The area of the Yukon and Northwest Territories is described and understood, but there is then a second part that tends to overrun the limits of the waters and includes a portion that might not be included within the continental shelf.
My colleagues have indicated that they fear that by introducing this definition the government has tended to weaken the arguments that Canada owns all of the north over which it has claimed entire sovereignty. I do not accept the argument put forward by the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin that by putting forward our amendment and discussing the weakness of our case we have perhaps done Canada irreparable harm. Does the hon. member feel that if you have been a serious deficiency in a bill you should not speak up in order to correct the mistake made by the government? Perhaps the hon. member possesses the mentality that thinks that all the brains of the country are held in monopoly by members on the government side, that government supported by the administration is the ultimate authority.
IMr. Lambert (Edmonton West.]
Perhaps the hon. member would subscribe to the point of view that was expressed by a former Minister of National Health and Welfare when he first proposed a national pension plan for Canada. The minister was heard to say, "This plan has been produced by the best brains in Canada; the others don't know what they are talking about". The fact is that that plan had four different versions and there was no relationship between the first plan and the one that was finally introduced. Therefore, I feel the hon. member is doing us a disservice when he suggests that we are wrong.

The contributions of the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Deakon) in this House are also noted for their infrequency. Perhaps he also thinks hon. members opposite have a monopoly on brains. As I was saying before the jackdaws crowed, our raising this point should not be taken as an indication that we have weakened Canada's position. It seemed to me that the purport of the hon. member's argument was that we had done Canada a disservice by pointing out this weakness. I do not think we have. I think there is another way to define what the government wants to do, without the introduction of this complication about which I have spoken.
Hon. members have indicated that it would have been better had the federal government been in a position to negotiate with those provinces which have continental shelves and are brought within the ambit of this bill. The bill does not affect Alberta or Saskatchewan, but I think that they, too, have an interest because all citizens of Canada have an inter-
March 9, 1970

est in the outcome of this whole question of offshore mineral rights and the control
thereof.
We are not concerned here only with the question of pollution; the bill goes far beyond pollution. Oil an gas conservation and production go far beyond pollution, as anyone who reads the new definition of a pipeline will see. Admittedly, one would have to use this legislation as the vehicle for controlling and finding safeguards against pollution in our offshore waters caused by exploration for oil, drilling for oil and subsequent production of oil and gas. I would also have thought that in addition to oil and gas we would have to consider controls that would have to be imposed as a result of the production of related materials, such as hydrocarbons and sulphur.
In any event, the view of my colleagues is that this bill should not be passed until an accord has been reached with the provinces on the matter. In effect, the federal government is asserting its authority here, even though it knows that it must make a deal with a number of the provinces. What the ultimate conclusion of the bargain will be, we do not know; the case for Nova Scotia may be quite different from that for British Columbia. Yet in all equity and fairness to Canadians, and to the citizens of the provinces concerned in particular, the settlement must be a uniform one.
Therefore, it seems to me that there is a strong case for deferring this bill until such time as the government has dealt with the matter. I do not see how the government can control pollution arising from offshore accidents to tankers under the terms of an act that deals with the conservation and production of oil and gas. The oil that was in the tanker recently wrecked off Nova Scotia had absolutely nothing to do with oil and gas that was produced on the continental shelf. This was an entirely different source of pollution.
I think there may be confusion in the minds of some hon. members who may think the act could serve as a vehicle for controlling offshore pollution by tankers. I hope this is not the case. However, it does seem to me that until an agreement is reached with the provinces, at least in principle, this bill is premature.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see no reason why this bill should
Oil and Gas Act
be delayed, because it appears to be a step in the right direction. For a long time Canadians took for granted that there must be a dividing boundary somewhere in the far Arctic

my guess would be, probably around the pole somewhere-and that everything on the Russian side of the pole belongs to Russia and everything on the Canadian side belongs to Canada. That was a very simple assumption to make because nobody was going there anyway, so it really did not make much difference.
I would be interested, however, in knowing what the Russians have decided to be their boundary. They are not quite as naive in respect of the Arctic as we are, and it is quite possible they have made some decision as to the boundary between Canada and the U.S.S.R. which is acceptable to them. I should like our government to indicate what that delineation might be, where the boundary is, and we can go on from there.
There is a general acceptance on the part of Canadians that we own the Arctic archipelago and are entitled to all the land in that area and the ice over it, and probably the transportation lanes through the ice. I was interested in the last day or two to note that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has again been playing that little game that Canadians are so prone to enjoy: he suggests we are the best; we are big, and we are important. In this regard he said that the United States could not protect its ships in the Arctic because they do not have the icebreakers. I am aware that a few years ago the Russians had an icebreaker that could travel many knots an hour breaking ice from six feet to twelve feet in depth. This made our icebreakers look pretty small. I think in fact their icebreaker was atomic-powered. If you remember, the Russians offered to break themselves into the port of Montreal and bring some of their ships in during the winter several years ago, but that offer was declined by Canada.
Recently I read an interesting article that may also have been read by other members. It referred to the fact that a ship, I believe owned by Australia, or perhaps by Sweden, had gone into the Antarctic and had stuck in the ice. It has been there for some length of time with several hundred people on board. The Russians have been trying to get to it, but have been unsuccessful. It was interesting that the United States has now been given permission to go into the icepack in the Antarctic in an attempt to get this ship out.

March 9, 1970
Oil and Gas Act
The United States does not seem to be the least bit worried about their icebreaker being able to work in that kind of ice. This indicates to me that they can probably do as well as we do in the Arctic if they are given the opportunity. The United States may have that opportunity unless we make some decisions fairly soon.
We have been told that we are the ones with the expertise in the Arctic. This makes everybody feel good, but probably it is not true. It certainly is not completely true: perhaps we should be told that as well. We are also told that we are giving consideration to this matter of our sovereignty in the Arctic and that the army is going to establish bases there. A few years ago when the radar chain-the Dew line-was established we were not even interested to the extent of maintaining our sovereignty there. In most cases we turned this operation over to the United States, with probably one Canadian there acting as an observer to maintain our claim to sovereignty in the area.
If we are serious about our development in the Arctic we will have to put people there. I am sympathetic to the feeling that the army is probably the most capable body to establish bases in that area and protect our claim to sovereignty, but it is necessary that we do so right away or we will wake up one morning to find that someone else has encroached on our sovereignty. This will probably be the consortium we have set up to drill for oil in the area.
The whole Arctic is very rich and most of its riches have been assessed. A lot of people from my riding are in the Arctic at all times. There are probably hundreds of people from the riding of Timiskaming in the Arctic in the summer. They are diamond-drilling and operating mining camps in that area. I was surprised to hear a nephew of mine, who worked several years ago in some of these places that we think of in a romantic sense, say that every rock you kick with your foot in the summertime contains heavy deposits of minerals including zinc and other metals. These minerals will eventually be produced there and will be of great importance in the development of the north.
We were not particularly concerned with the problems of the north and our sovereignty in that area until a former Minister of Northern Affairs established a consortium of a oil companies in conjunction with the federal government. This was a step in the right direction: it allowed Canadians to participate

directly in the development of the area. It has now resulted in blocking out very large oil and gas reserves for the Canadian public.
There is a problem raised in respect of this bill regarding the division of jurisdiction in the north. We have the federal government in the territories, with provincial governments exercising sovereignty over the land adjacent to the sea where there is great interest in the continental shelf. Other members have mentioned the Law of the Sea, the decision of the Geneva convention in relation to the continental shelf and the complexities of that problem. The problem in the Arctic today is rather like the problem resulting from early inhabitants in this country who went to various parts of Canada and settled: as a result of being there, they claimed ownership of the area. Throughout most areas squatters claims were as good as any because of the application of the law of possession.
The suggestion that possession was nine-tenths of the law in establishing ownership was certainly borne out in many parts of Canada and has been the criteria for decisions as to ownership. Therefore, if we are bold enough to establish our rights to the Arctic archipelago, the seas between the islands and the mainland, and our rights in respect of the continental shelf in that area, we will probably have a good claim. If we do not establish that sovereignty in the north, a claim will be exercised, to some extent at least, by the people who take possession. To a great degree possession will be taken by companies based other than in Canada which have purchased large tracts of the area for exploration. They will be established there and will have some right to the gas and oil if such is found in the territories. These resources will in fact be lost to us.
We have also heard a great deal in the last few weeks about oil pollution. It is very easy to talk about oil pollution and the danger it will create in the Arctic. It scares the pants off anybody who thinks about the danger that exists in the Gulf of Mexico and other areas with warm climates and high water temperatures, such as California, and the dangers that exist in the colder waters off Nova Scotia and British Columbia. We cannot assess the dangers that exist from oil pollution in the north.
Oil pollution is almost as certain to follow as day follows night if we do not exercise extreme control over transportation facilities in the area. In my opinion, if this government was at all responsible it would quit playing around with Humble Oil and tankers in the
March 9, 1970

Oil and Gas Act
Arctic. This attitude will lead, without doubt, to a tragedy there which will set back for many years the development of the area. The government should get on with the business of developing a pipeline from the coast, through the Northwest Territories, to bring oil into central Canada. In my opinion this would probably satisfy the minister's desire to establish a continental energy policy. I suggest, although this is not the inevitable result of establishing a pipeline, that if a pipeline were established from the Mackenzie River delta south to Edmonton even before a commodity is available to be carried in that pipeline, it would have a great deal of influence on the development of other pipelines such as the one contemplated across the Yukon and Alaska to the west coast.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
It will have a great effect on whether or not it is considered to be to the advantage of the companies which wish to move this resource to even consider the development of tankers for the Arctic. I think if we have the foresight to instal a pipeline and put in the facilities, there would be many advantages. A small pipeline has been in existence in that vicinity for many years: it runs from Norman Wells through the Canol project. This oil line has proven to be feasible. The temperatures are not prohibitive for transportation by pipeline in that area.
The fact that we now have a very large reserve of natural gas will probably make the transportation of oil easier. I suggest that in Canada we should be thinking of building a pipeline either in consortium with the oil industry or, if necessary, alone. If the scientists and others who have spoken about the dangers from pollution in the Arctic are correct when they indicate that we have no method by which to cope with the pollution problem, it behooves all of us to consider an alternate method such as a pipeline from that area to connect with the existing transportation facilities out of Edmonton and through the oil and gas distribution system that is now in effect. This would mean we would have to run a pipeline across Canada as well. I think it is time consideration were given to this matter.
I have spoken to the officials of some pipeline companies. As recently as a week ago they told me that the cost of such a system was beyond their capability. The companies that are now transporting our oil from west to east into Ontario do not have the facilities
to put in a reasonably sized pipeline to handle the requirements of eastern Canada which would make us less dependent on exports to the United States via a southerly route.
If we were to bring the known reserves from the Arctic through the Edmonton distribution point without having a system of disposing of it when it was brought into the normal stream, the situation would be chaotic. So I suggest the government should give consideration to a pipeline which, it seems to me, would eliminate the necessity of the use of surface and submarine tankers as well as the necessity of demanding that the Humble Oil Company take certain precautions in respect of the Manhattan. We are aware of the damage the Manhattan suffered. We are also aware of the desire of the Minister of Transport that the company instal emergency connections so that the oil may be pumped out of that ship if there should be an accident. I suggest we should not allow that ship to go back into the Arctic for the purpose of transporting oil if danger is contemplated.
I am not opposed to the United States government cooperating with us in examining the feasibility of this type of transportation, but all tankers are not similar to the Manhattan. Tankers which meet very minimum standards may be sailing in there. Even when sailing on the high seas, such tankers have been known to break up. One of them broke up on the high seas off the coast of Africa, where limited restrictions are in force. If such ships are taken into the Arctic, the situation could be chaotic. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) will have to co-operate in respect of the development of oil in that area. The problem is not so small that there will be any difficulty involved in having two ministers engaged in it.
These two ministers will have an opportunity to do something in respect of the development of Canada which will bring great rewards for many years to come. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) pointed out the large volume of oil that has already been assessed in that area. In my opinion the size of this resource should point up the necessity for establishing a reasonably sized pipeline from the Mackenzie delta. That area is free of ice for a sufficient number of months that we would not have the problems that exist in the Arctic. Certainly, such a program would eliminate some of the fears we have. Along such a pipeline communities

would develop. Although I am sure the government will not change its policy, I was very interested to hear some of the arguments brought forward the other day by the oil lobby people in respect of the unfairness of the policy requiring the hiring of indigents in the area. They pointed out that this caused some difficulty. They stated that because of this fact they were not meeting the schedules they would like to meet. Tough bananas!

speechtext:
That may be so, but it is too bad for these people. By law they must hire a certain number of the local inhabitants. Once these people are trained, I am sure there will be permanent employment for them if we use the resources we have. I suppose the building of a pipeline in the area would be a very expensive proposition. It would provide a good deal of temporary employment. Also, the operation of a pipeline on the permafrost would involve the employment of a number of employees on a permanent basis. It seems to me that everyone should be interested in the development of an orderly market for oil and gas. I believe it would be much better if the oil and gas could be introduced through a common denominator such as Edmonton or Calgary.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
With such a point of connection with the existing facilities which will be bringing in oil from the north, we would be able to utilize and distribute more evenly the potential of the area from which we now receive the major part of our gas and oil. We would be able to extend and equalize the flow from both the Arctic and the local area which have been serving the needs of Canada and the United States for some years and which must have difficulty meeting the demand at peak periods. This difficulty would be partially solved if we added this large resource which in many cases will only be passing through the area.
I imagine that the Americans who are operating the oil discoveries in Prudhoe Bay would be willing to move their oil and gas resources through the same pipeline, through the Canadian distribution system, provided it found its way directly to the United States, with the transportation cost being the only requirement for its Canadians transmission. I think this system could be arranged. I believe

we have been very shortsighted in the development of our resources.
We all agree that the danger of oil pollution in the Arctic is almost insurmountable. There is no question in my mind that if tankers in that area were to provide the major source of transportation, disaster would follow disaster. The ice in that area shifts very rapidly. There will be periods when channels which are not supposed to be clear will be clear, and periods when channels which are supposed to be clear will not be clear. A tanker getting stuck in that area will face the difficulties which experts indicate will always be with us. I suggest, therefore, that we send this matter to committee.
I should like the government to consider the establishment of an overland transportation facility to the Arctic. The resources in that area are immense, and because they are immense we will all live to see the day when we establish cities in the Arctic such as the cities of Siberia. These cities will not be established there as the result of someone's dream, but as a result of economic need and feasibility.
Cities covered with glass have been recommended for the Arctic before. They are now in existence in many areas of Russia. It has been interesting-and I have heard much criticism of it-to watch Ab Douglas as he travels across Siberia, to find that Siberia is not the Arctic as we know it and that the development that has taken place in that area is based mainly on the resource industry. I am sure this kind of development will take place in Canada if the government will show initiative by introducing legislation which will make it feasible.
I do not expect the present government to set about drawing up a plan for an orderly development of the resources in the Arctic. However, I do not think it is seeking too much to ask it to consider an alternative transportation method that will meet the needs of the foreseeable future, so far as gas and oil are concerned, by building a pipeline from that area to our main outlets. The government should supply some of the money and the direction that would make this possible.
The Minister of Transport has been very brave in commenting on what he will do and how he will go about it. He says it is not gunboat diplomacy. Perhaps it is not, but I wonder how he is going to enforce legislation. I think the Humble Oil Company has been very generous to Canada. They could proba-
March 9, 1970

Oil and Gas Act
bly buy most of the Arctic if they wished. They have been very generous in saying they will make the 30 or 40 changes to their ship; they will build special compartments to comply with Canadian regulations, and they will do all this for the sake of the development, which may not even take place.
This is very good and the Canadian people are quite pleased that the Minister of Transport has taken this kind of action. But I think they would be just as pleased if action were taken by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who has not had the opportunity since he took on that portfolio to do anything of great importance in his own field. In fact, not much has been done by his department since the Trans-Canada pipeline was inaugurated.
I think he would find some support if he were to suggest at least that a feasibility study be carried out by the Committee, in conjunction with a study of this bill, of the development of an alternative program for the building of a pipeline from the Arctic, which would eliminate many of the problems which I think everyone agrees are evident. I do not really expect miracles and I do not expect that suddenly the government will be seized with a vision. If they were, I think they would be very surprised at the response they would receive from the Canadian public.
I can remember when another vision of the north caught on very well. Most people in Canada are sympathetic to the development that is going on there. The fact that northern development is discussed in the House as much as wheat is an indication that there is an interest in our northern resources and a willingness on the part of the Canadian public to participate in their development.
We are again allowing the Americans to provide an alternative that will not cost us anything and that will dispose of one of our products. But we have not really done much for ourselves. I think the minister would find a goal for himself if he were responsible to the Canadian public for the handling of the vast resources which we have in the Arctic and were to provide a means of transportation that would be free of the perils that most people believe endanger the present system.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take about five minutes to express my interest in the intent of this bill. At present, and for a number of years, the search for oil and gas on the continental shelf of the east coast of Canada has been rather
academic. Companies interested in this matter, procure a licence from the appropriate provincial governments and one from the federal government and proceed to do exploratory drilling.
Since no significant discovery of oil or gas has been made in that area up to the present, it would seem people are content with what is happening. But I submit that there is a need for a great deal of work in this area by the government of Canada. If in the near future there were important discoveries of oil or gas on the continental shelf on the eastern side of Canada, there would be tremendous complications among the different economic interests following the discovery. It is late to do so now, but it would be wise to resolve these jurisdictional responsibilities before gas and oil are discovered in commercial quantities in the area.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
It is true the five Atlantic provinces have not decided among themselves where the lines of jurisdiction should lie as between the various provinces, on the assumption that they have the jurisdiction over mineral and oil and gas rights on the continental shelf. But the federal government does not admit their claim, and you have a situation where there is a dispute as to jurisdiction between the federal government on the one hand and the five eastern provinces on the other.
Then you have a potential difficulty between Canada on the one hand and the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon on the other. You have the question of where the division line of jurisdiction lies on the continental shelf between Canada and the United States in the George's Bank area. None of these questions have yet been resolved. If that were not enough, this bill introduces another question of jurisdiction as between the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) on the one hand and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) on the other. I can visualize situations where it would not be clear which minister had jurisdiction. I am not sure, for example, what the position of Hudson Bay is, and I would not be sure what the position would be in Hudson Strait-for example, which minister is responsible.
If oil or gas is discovered in commercial quantities in the near future, it will be of tremendous potential importance. It should be of tremendous economic benefit to an area of Canada that has not shared fairly in the
4568

March 9, 1970
Oil and Gas Act
development of our country over the last few decades, and surely the development should be in a manner which would be of benefit to those provinces. Secondly, it would be adjacent to a part of North America which is deficient in gas and oil at the present time. And I might mention, Mr. Speaker, that the geological indications of the continental shelf off eastern Canada look quite promising for gas and oil. If they are found there in commercial quantities, there is an immediate tremendous market and therefore tremendous pressure for immediate development in the area because, as hon. members know, all of eastern Canada is supplied with oil from overseas, chiefly from South America. The same is true of the eastern seaboard of the United States.
So it is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that the discovery of oil in that area would be of tremendous importance immediately and there would be very immediate pressure to develop it at once. Therefore, it is vitally important that the government of Canada resolve these questions of jurisdiction as rapidly as possible so there will be a clear delineation of responsibility before discoveries are made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is maintained by hon. members directly across the House that the bill before us, S-5, in some way diminishes Canada's claim to sovereignty over the waters adjacent to our sea coast, particularly those in the Arctic. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) in particular stated he was not opposed to Bill S-5 for technical reasons, but because "it amounts to a serious diminution of Canadian sovereignty over the waters of the Arctic." This is simply not so. As a matter of fact, obstructing the passage of this bill will in itself have the effect of diminishing Canadian offshore claims. However, these are not claims of sovereignty over waters. These are claims of sovereign rights to explore for, develop and exploit the natural resources of the sea bed and subsoil of Canada's continental margin.
Perhaps I might spend a few minutes for the purpose of clearly differentiating between first, Canada's claims to sovereignty over waters lying off our coasts and, second, Canada's sovereign rights to exploit the natural resources of our continental margin. Canada lays claim to sovereignty over waters off our sea coasts where they are internal waters or historic waters forming an integral part of Canada and where they fall within
March 3, 1970

the limits of our territorial sea. Under international law, Canada's internal waters are those on the landward side of the base lines from which Canada's territorial sea is measured, and Canada's territorial sea comprises a marginal three-mile wide belt measured from the coastline, or from straight base lines joining headlands and offshore islands established pursuant to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act of 1964.
The promulgation of such straight base lines involves the seaward extension of Canada's exclusive competence beyond its present limits vis-a-vis other countries. Since this exclusive competence includes proprietary as well as jurisdictional rights, there is no question as to Canada's ownership of the mineral resources of the sea bed and subsoil underlying these waters.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
In Bill S-5, we are not dealing with problems of sovereignty over waters. Bill S-5 is concerned with mineral resources, in particular the oil and gas resources, of the sea bed and subsoil of Canada's continental margin. Under the terms of the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf of 1958, Canada can claim the natural resources of the sea bed and subsoil for offshore areas extending off the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic coasts far beyond the limits of the territorial sea. The shelf convention is the instrument of international law that confirms the exclusive right of a sovereign state to explore for and exploit these natural resources off its seacoasts wherever it can manage to do so. Thus, Canada asserts exclusive rights, sovereign rights as the shelf convention calls them, over the natural resources of her continental margin extending far beyond the possible limits of Canadian sovereignty over the waters adjacent to our coasts.
I should mention here that Canada is probably the most aggressive nation in the world in asserting her rights to offshore mineral resources. We have issued oil and gas permits covering more than half the total area of Canada's continental margin. Hon. members may recall that our continental margin comprises a total area of about 1.5 million square miles, almost 40 per cent as large as the entire land area of Canada. Thus, the total area covered by oil and gas permits issued to date off our seacoasts is the equivalent of 20 to 25 per cent of Canada's total land area. This is about twice as large as the maximum area that might be considered favourable for
Oil and Gas Act
petroleum exploration in the four western provinces combined.
To illustrate Canada's diligence in asserting our rights in the offshore, I would like to point out that federal oil and gas permits have been issued off the east coast extending in an unbroken stretch of some 2,000 miles from the Gulf of Maine region through the Grand Banks and thence to Hudson Strait. These permits extend seaward as far as 425 miles east from Newfoundland. We have issued permits off the west coast over a stretch of 500 miles from the Strait of Juan de Fuca region to the Dixon Entrance region, and we have issued permits covering the bulk of Hudson Bay. In the Arctic region, which seems to be the main matter of concern to hon. members directly opposite, approximately 150 million acres of oil and gas permits have been issued in the Arctic offshore. These are situated in the Beaufort Sea region, where they extend as far seaward as 140 miles off the mainland coast, and in the Arctic islands region where they cover most of the channels between the various islands.
One can hardly say that the federal government has not been aggressive in this field. In fact, there has been some tendency of late by various parties, including some members of the United Nations, to find fault with us on this account. If hon. members will refer to Bill S-5, they will note that clause 3(b) states that the act applies in respect of oil and gas inthose submarine areas adjacent to the cost of Canada to a water depth of 200 metres or beyond that limit to where the depth of the superjacent waters admits of the exploitation of the natural resources of the seabed and subsoil thereof.
There is no stipulation here, as has been stated by hon. members opposite, that there is a 200-metre water depth limitation. The wording of clause 3(b) is taken almost verbatim from the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf, which clearly states that the exploitable depth is the governing factor. Technology is continually moving this flexible "exploitable depth" boundary farther seaward. Each of the two semi-submersible drilling units currently being built in Halifax will have a drilling capability of 25,000 feet and the ability to operate in water depths well in excess of 200 metres, and technology is fast evolving methods of completing and producing oil wells commercially in water depths of this magnitude.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ALL SASKATCHEWAN AS DESIGNATED AREA
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ALL SASKATCHEWAN AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 5 I put the following question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand):
In view of the fact that Saskatchewan is facing a deepening economic crisis, is the minister now prepared to consider the inclusion of the entire province under the Regional Development Incentives Act?
I asked this question for a number of reasons because the province of Saskatchewan is, in fact, in a very bad economic situation at the present time. It is a deepening financial crisis, and because of that my colleagues and I from Saskatchewan believe that the entire province should qualify for any additional help and aid that may be coming under the new Regional Development Incentives Program.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
A short time ago-say three or four years ago-Saskatchewan in many ways was a "have" province. Now, because of our agricultural crisis, Saskatchewan is not a "have" province. Saskatchewan and its people are suffering, in one way or another, the consequences of the province's economic crisis. An
March 9, 1970

economic recession is well advanced in Saskatchewan. I shall try in the few minutes I am allowed to speak this evening to outline why I think all that province ought to be included as a special, designated area under the program.
As I said before, the province's crisis affects everybody living in the province, but first and foremost it affects the farmers. Farm income has dropped drastically and many farmers are being forced off the land. As a matter of fact, the way of life of many people is being changed drastically. Statistics show that in the first half of 1969, for example farm income was down by 40 per cent as compared with 1968. The Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) has also told us that there will be no final wheat payment this year, a factor which will add to the problems confronting Saskatchewan farmers.
Those who do not work on farms are also feeling the effect of the economic recession. The average weekly wage has dropped relatively. In 1963, for example, the average weekly wage in Saskatchewan was below the national average only by $3.95. In the first six months of 1969 the average weekly wage had fallen to $9.85 below the national average. As you can see, the average weekly wage is falling further below the national average weekly wage.
Widespread unemployment is another consequence of Saskatchewan's economic crisis. Unemployment now is higher than it has been for a number of years. Retail sales across the province are down; the first 11 months of 1969 saw a drop in retail sales of over $100 million. These figures do not tell the entire story because the businessmen and people of small communities are much harder hit than the people living in the larger centres.
The farm machinery industry is perhaps the hardest hit industry. Many farm machinery dealers have already pulled out of Saskatchewan and others are contemplating this action. Capital investment in the province is down drastically, while in Manitoba and Alberta capital investment has increased as compared with last year. Also, the population of Saskatchewan has declined. As a matter of fact, the only thing we are exporting these days is people; we are certainly not exporting wheat. Between April and October, 1969, 10,500 people left Saskatchewan at an average rate of 1,800 per month.
Hon. members know how well this fact alone indicates the severity of the problem we
Proceedings in Adjournment Motion face. The very future of Saskatchewan is at stake. Including the province in the new plan would be of help to the people of Saskatchewan. Rumour has it, Mr. Speaker, that both Saskatoon and Regina may be included very shortly in the regional development incentive plan. Of course, we are in favour of this, but I hope the government will consider including the whole province in the plan.
In the fairly densely populated area I represent, many people living in towns and villages cannot find work. Many farmers who seek employment off the farm to supplement their income also cannot find work. Whatever form the regional development incentive plan may take, it ought not to take the form of mere paper tokenism. A plan on paper is not enough, because we must bring industry to the province.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion could utilize this plan to bring about national unity in Canada. National unity is not simply a matter of bilingualism and biculturalism but involves matters touching on the social and economic life of the people of this country as well. All regions of Canada must be equal partners within confederation. The government could do much toward solving the province's problems by including the entire province under the regional development incentive program. I ask the government, again, to give serious consideration to including the entire province. There is a grave emergency there and the province will warrant special attention until such time as it extricates itself from the economic recession. Unless the province receives that attention it may not extricate itself from the recession for many years, in which case the income base of the people will be destroyed and their way of life changed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Martin P. O'Connell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ALL SASKATCHEWAN AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all agreed in this House as to the seriousness of the economic situation in Saskatchewan. I know it is the feeling of my hon. friends on this side that the resources of the government must be brought to bear to alleviate the unique financial and other strains thrust in little over a year on Canadians in the prairie provinces, and on none more so than in Saskatchewan.
Saskatchewan has suffered a relatively sudden and drastic reversal in economic well-being. I can assure the hon. member and other members of the House that for its part the Department of Regional Economic Expan-
March 9, 1970

Proceedings in Adjournment Motion sion intends to ensure in short order that its resources and programs under its two pieces of legislation contribute in the most effective way possible to improving the economic situation in that province.
The task is to assist not only in meeting the short-term urgent situation which has developed over the past two years but to carry out a longer term industrialization and diversification of the province's economy. My minister has informed the House on a number of recent occasions that he hopes before the end of this month to complete agreements with the provinces to designate special areas jointly selected by the federal government and the provincial governments in which joint economic development plans will operate-plans	in which the department's
resources play a very significant role, a more significant role than in the designated regions.
I can say that the question of the role of the department in Saskatchewan has been the subject of close examination in the past few months and that discussions with the province of Saskatchewan have sought to find the most effective role for the department in light of the economic situation there and in view of the potential in Saskatchewan for economic expansion and diversification.
This federal role has to be meshed with the province's own economic development programs. We are fully aware of the urgency of the Saskatchewan situation. It is particularly urgent that we should set our course there at the earliest possible date, because programs of industrialization take some time to gather momentum. I believe a decision as to that course will be made in the very near future.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-CHARLOTTETOWN-PROPOSED TRANSFER OF CERTAIN MARINE AGENCY FUNCTIONS AND PERSONNEL
TRANSPORT-CHARLOTTETOWN-PROPOSED TRANSFER OF CERTAIN MARINE AGENCY FUNCTIONS AND PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time I have been concerned about the diminution of the staff of the Charlottetown marine agency of the Department of Transport. My question of February 24, on which this debate is based, was not my first inquiry on the subject.
There has been a regrettable flurry of rumours and a war of nerves in connection with the fate and future of the Charlottetown marine agency. First there were the stories that one of the ships of the agency was to be transferred out of Charlottetown. After much anxiety and speculation we were given the word that this was not to take place, at least not at the present time.

Now, as a result of the exploits and investigations of yet another task force, it is alleged to be the accounting and engineering division which is to be transferred to another centre. Indeed, a former employee of the Department of Transport in Charlettetown has publicly declared that the move will take place and that June 1 is D-day-diminution day or debarkation day, whatever one wishes to call it. Certainly for the employees it will be debarkation from Prince Edward Island, where they have been performing their duties well and in many cases for a long time. The man who made this statement subsequently resigned from the department.
* (10:10 p.m.)
One of the developments which brought me the greatest satisfaction when I was a government-supporting MP was the building of a new wharf and agency headquarters at Charlottetown. The project took a long time and was not completed until the government I supported had left office. But the splendid headquarters, which I am told are modern, well equipped and practically new, capable of allowing personnel to discharge their duties efficiently and well, stand there-and it is shocking, surprising and totally inexplicable why the personnel therein should be diminished. Why any division of the department should be moved has not yet been demonstrated or declared.
Charlottetown has long been the site of a marine agency, and it is the logical location for a marine agency. But in recent years there have been gradual decreases in its role and function. For instance, purchases which used to be made in Charlottetown on a very satisfactory basis are now being made elsewhere.
We grow weary of these cutbacks in the operation of the dominion government in our province. The closing of the Queen Charlotte naval base was one; the valuable enamel and heating project at the Charlottetown airport brought much needed employment to our city. It had a helpful effect upon our economy, but it too went the way of the naval base. From time to time other aspects of the federal government program are being curtailed or withdrawn. It has happened in the Post Office; and I mean at headquarters, not just the closing of small offices.
The fur research station and biological research have been cut back, and there have also been cutbacks in the maintenance of fishing harbours. All of these mark a decline in the operations of the federal government,
March. 9, 1970

producing a shrinkage of employment and loss of economic strength. We have only to look at the estimates for the coming year to see how low a priority Prince Edward Island has with the government.
I ask that this sort of thing end. Strange, indeed, it is to plan a special regional expansion program-for which, incidentally, our province pays two-thirds of the cost-and at the same time to allow other federal government departments to contribute to economic decline and to unemployment which the plan of the regional expansion department is designed to ameliorate and overcome. It seems to me that a recognition of the ills of continuing disparity among the regions of Canada should not be confined to one department of government but should be known and acted upon by all.
Therefore, let the spokesman for the minister give his assurance on this item at least. Let us know that there will not be a depletion of the minister's staff at Charlottetown. Let the minister also use his influence to curtail the cutbacks, of which Prince Edward Island has already undergone more than its share. To use a recently resurrected expression currently getting some coverage in the United States, "More benign neglect we can do without". But even benign neglect is less hurtful than this kind of attention and disruption.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSPORT-CHARLOTTETOWN-PROPOSED TRANSFER OF CERTAIN MARINE AGENCY FUNCTIONS AND PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question raised by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) may I say that there was an article in the newspaper recently that did speculate with rumours. I know there is never smoke without fire. Nevertheless, I am afraid I cannot tell the hon. member that something will be done or will not be done, because no decision has yet been taken by the department.
Some quite extensive changes in the Department of Transport have been announced. Week after week and month after month the department is looking to see what it can do to give better service to the public. When changes are made, it is sometimes necessary to move employees around or to change them; this is unavoidable. The department is not trying to do something that is going to hurt the economy of the country or to jeopardize giving good service to the public. But still it is not a fact yet because, as I have said, no decision has been taken.
The deputy minister wrote the hon. member on January 26 last in reference to this matter. There is one sentence in this
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion letter which I think covers everything. It is as follows:
We are constantly reviewing our organization in an effort to improve our efficiency and our service to the public.
I think every member of the House of Commons should work with that in mind, that every department of the Canadian government should do everything in order to give better service to the public. In a letter written in reply to the Premier of Prince Edward Island the Minister of Transport assured the Premier of that province by saying:
Several years ago, in an effort to improve our efficiency and our service to the public, we established a maritime regional administration. We are now studying the possibility of providing certain common services more economically. I can assure you however that, contrary to press reports, no decisions have been taken, nor will there be until they are reviewed carefully with myself and officials of my department.
Still there is no decision taken, and I do not see that a decision will be taken shortly in the sense that the hon. member for Hillsborough mentioned a while ago. He has asked that the minister give him and the people of his riding the assurance that there will not be any change. I cannot give that assurance to the hon. member, but I can tell him that the Department of Transport is trying to do the best to give the people of P.E.I. good service.

maintopic: TRADE-SALE OF ATOMIC ENERGY PLANT TO ROUMANIA-CONTINGENT CONDITIONS
TRADE-SALE OF ATOMIC ENERGY PLANT TO ROUMANIA-CONTINGENT CONDITIONS
speechtext:
The other day when I raised a question about the sale of an atomic energy plant to Rou-mania, Mr. Speaker suggested that there was not urgency in respect of this program, or at least not as he saw it. I should like to read a small excerpt from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 7 which says that Roumanian officials are presently in Canada engaged in talks with Canadian officials regarding this sale. This article suggests that West Germany is also interested in the sale, so in fact we have a competitor. The article states:
The talks involve a $100,000,000 generating station and fuel fabricating plant and, possibly, a $50,000,000 plant to produce heavy water-
So you can see this is an important item to this sector of Canada's industrial economy. If we were successful in building a plant for this country, we might also sell others. I suggest this is quite an urgent matter. I come from a section of the country about which
March 9, 1970
4574	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion agricultural and trade officials were not concerned regarding the sale of wheat until we woke up one morning and found somebody else had the markets. This is a very important item and the government should consider it very carefully.
There is one item in respect of which I should specifically like to compliment and congratulate those responsible. At the Douglas Point atomic energy plant they were successful in performing an on-power refuelling. This was only partial, but it was something new and it was successful. If the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) had anything to do with this operation, I extend my congratulations to him as well. If I were purchasing an atomic energy plant from Canada or any other country, I would be concerned about the conditions of sale. I would want to know whether the plant would work. I asked specifically in my question the other day about these conditions of sale.
The next item involves heavy water. After considering Canada's experience in this respect, I have some doubt. We have built, or are in the process of building a heavy water plant in Nova Scotia. The federal government has washed its hands of it but Atomic Energy of Canada signed a contract. At the very least, I suggest this was a very sloppy business approach. There were no penalties involved in the contract in respect of the delivery of heavy water. If they did not approve the new method of production. I would ask why Atomic Energy signed the contract. The story has been the same in Nova Scotia. I do not believe Atomic Energy of Canada or the government has anything to brag about in this regard. The sale of atomic energy plants abroad is involved, and a doubt is cast on the ability of Canadian industry generally.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I suggest that the federal government should get on the ball and do something about the problem. I believe if I were inquiring in Canada about a plant of this nature, I would be concerned about the technical know-how of the people involved. The federal government has decided not to proceed with the intense neutron generator which would have supplied us with further knowledge in this particular field. If I were purchasing a plant and was told I would probably be able to upgrade it, and that instead of using uranium I might be able to have a fast-breeder reactor which would use plutoni-


um, or that I would be able to sell plutonium to some other country by purchasing a plant from Canada, I would be very interested.
At the present time I would be very uneasy as a buyer. Our research and development percentagewise in respect of our gross national product is not in any way comparable to that of Great Britain or the United States. I suggest we need to invest our money in this area. If financing is a condition of sale, I suggest that perhaps we should subsidize the financing if this is required. I have one last comment to make in respect of the standardization of equipment. As I understand it, we produce an atomic plant of one kind and other types are produced in other parts of the world. I hope ours is a good one. If we are not successful in our sales abroad in respect of our particular style of atomic energy plant, I believe it is high time we took a real look at the atomic energy situation in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: TRADE-SALE OF ATOMIC ENERGY PLANT TO ROUMANIA-CONTINGENT CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has ranged far and wide from the question he asked the other day, but certainly some of his contributions are useful. I was particularly glad to see his support for our atomic energy program and his encouragement in respect of our spending more money in this area. If he would be my advocate for the Treasury Board in this area, I think that would be extremely useful. I remind him, however, of the fact that we had to cut back on some of our basic research in areas which might ultimately lead to technology in respect of fast-breeding reactors. Part of the problem is being a small country. We can only afford a certain amount of science. We do not have an open end. Our science spending is not tied to defence spending as it is in the United States.
I suggest that as much as possible we keep in the areas in which we have expertise. I believe that in the field of atomic reactors we have great expertise. We have a scientific team which is second to none. Certainly in the future we can be in the vanguard in the world and possibly achieve a considerable self-sufficiency in the energy field if we have confidence in and support this team which has done so well in the past.
The hon. member specifically asked the other day whether or not our on-power refuelling of the Douglas Point reactor was a condition contingent upon any sale of an atomic energy plant to Roumania. On-power refuelling is one of the real merits of the Canadian Candu system, and our scientists should be given great credit for achieving
March 9, 1970	COMMONS
this. The plants being offered for sale to Rou-mania and elsewhere do in fact contain this outstanding feature, but it was not a condition of the sale to Roumania.
I think the hon. member has done a service in bringing this matter to the forefront today. Because we have had some problem in respect of on-power refuelling, some people have lost confidence in the reactor program and have some doubt as to whether we should continue. Speaking for the government, may I say I can think of nothing that would do more harm to our country than for us to lose faith in this reactor at the present time, when so much has been put into it and when we have achieved a place in science second to none in the world.

We must bear in mind that other countries have had at least as many problems as we have had in this very new science of atomic energy and reactors. I sincerely hope and have confidence that the Canadian people will not lose faith in this regard and that this House and its members will not be tempted to not follow through with this program. I think it would definitely put us back if we did not follow through with this excellent program in respect of our Canadian reactor, which I think will be of great benefit to Canadian people in the years to come.
